LegalOn halves Codex costs while maintaining development speed

📅 08 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1133 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • LegalOn cut costs by 65% while maintaining development speed by matching Astra, Sol, and Luna to tasks and managing budgets strategically.
  • It has been revealed that legalOn Technologies offers Professional AI globally, using AI to support legal work and other key business functions.
  • This approach extends beyond its products to making the organization itself AI-native.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

LegalOn cut costs by 65% while maintaining development speed by matching Astra, Sol, and Luna to tasks and managing budgets strategically.

Cost reduction in mature business areas.

Reduction in estimated daily costs.

It has been revealed that legalOn Technologies offers Professional AI globally, using AI to support legal work and other key business functions. By combining domain expertise with AI, it enables people to focus on complex judgments and decisions. Its goal is AI-driven management that improves the quality and speed of business decision-making.

This approach extends beyond its products to making the organization itself AI-native. The manufacturer integrated Codex into its development process and expanded adoption across the organization through day-to-day use.

In a recent development, as adoption took hold, a newly introduced challenge emerged: cost control. Unlimited use of high-performance models could drive up spending, while blanket restrictions risked undermining the productivity gains AI had enabled.

According to recent reports, how could it reduce costs without slowing development? LegalOn Technologies addressed this challenge by selecting among GPT‑6 (Astra, Luna) and GPT‑6.1 Sol based on task complexity and development stage, and aligning budgets with each business’s stage of growth. The firm halved costs while maintaining development speed.

The firm initially gave developers unlimited access to its main model, GPT‑5.5 in Fast mode. They expanded its use to design, implementation, and everyday work, learning through experimentation how best to divide responsibilities between people and AI.

Continuing to use high-performance models without limits, however, would inevitably exceed the annual budget. The tech giant's AI-powered Development CoE (AID CoE) began developing guidelines for model selection. AID CoE tested and monitored models, while managers shared its findings with their teams. This enabled each engineer to independently choose the most suitable model for each task.

In a recent development, the new guidelines shifted the company from using the highest-capability model for every task to choosing the right model for the job. Teams started with a lightweight model and moved to more capable models as task complexity increased.

To support governance, the company also introduced system controls through administrator settings, with monthly usage limits for departments and individuals. AID CoE monitors usage and adjusts limits as business needs require.

Internal testing under these controls helped make the selection criteria more specific. GPT‑6 Luna, the lightest model, handles code implementation with clear requirements; GPT‑6.1 Sol supports standard design, data analysis, and document preparation; and GPT‑6 Astra, the most capable model, handles advanced judgment, including architecture design. Matching models to tasks gradually became a shared practice across teams.

Everyday execution and implementation; running everyday automations; delegating relatively simple tasks and analysis; code implementation, mainly as a subagent.

Standard design and analysis; relatively simple software design; routine numerical analysis and document creation; tasks requiring shorter completion times than with Luna.

Complex analysis, design, and orchestration; complex analysis and document creation; complex software design; coordinating agents as the orchestrator.

Alongside model selection, the manufacturer began restricting Fast mode by default, allowing individual requests only when needed. Although the change raised concerns about development speed, teams used approaches such as running tasks in parallel to maintain performance and transition smoothly.

It also introduced budget caps for AI spending at the department, group, and individual levels. The established LegalOn business was asked to improve cost efficiency by up to approximately 20%, while newly introduced businesses in the launch phase received generous budgets to encourage active use of AI.

Sources indicate that yuta Tokitake, Senior Engineering Manager at LegalOn Technologies, explains that latest businesses prioritized business speed over cost efficiency. The aim was to use AI extensively to increase output and ultimately drive business growth.

Together, model selection, feature restrictions, and budgets tailored to each business reduced estimated daily costs by approximately 65%. This approach kept the overall budget under control while directing resources toward businesses the organization wanted to grow.

Model optimization and strategic resource allocation delivered the following results:.

A shift from using the most capable model for every task to selecting GPT‑6 Astra, GPT‑6.1 Sol, or GPT‑6 Luna based on task complexity and development stage.

Development performance maintained after restricting Fast mode by default, supported by team practices such as parallel task execution.

Budget caps that combined approximately 20% greater efficiency in mature businesses with active investment in upcoming businesses.

A 65% reduction in estimated daily costs compared with GPT‑5.5 by choosing among GPT‑6 and 6.1 models.

Recent findings suggest that through model optimization, the firm reduced costs without sacrificing development speed or quality. Teams are also seeing AI steadily shorten the cycle from development to release.

But the manufacturer is looking further ahead. Does faster development alone make AI investment a success? The connection between faster development and customer value remained unclear. “It is almost a given that AI can accelerate system development and updates,” notes Tokitake. “What we really want to understand is whether that faster development actually translates into value for customers.”.

This question prompted the firm to develop its own metric, shifting the basis for evaluating AI investment from development speed and usage volume to customer value.

In a recent development, tokitake explains: “When using AI, we can track the cost of individual tasks, but the total cost of a complete piece of work—a feature release—often remains a black box. So we designed the measurement around each feature release as a single unit. By linking the customer value that release delivers to the actual AI costs invested in it, we aim to make the return on investment visible and accurate.”.

The company is right now building the pipeline to calculate this metric. Once complete, it will make the true ROI in terms of customer value visible. LegalOn Technologies is moving beyond AI cost management toward directly connecting technology investment with business value.

In a recent development, the next goal is to turn individual engineers' AI know-how into an organization-wide capability. As a first step, the manufacturer looks to build a knowledge base to collect and share practical experience. It will capture knowledge such as the best model combinations for design, implementation, and review, and promptly turn individual successes into company-wide best practices.

Industry observers note that these changes, driven by teams' practical experience, are also shaping the organization and hiring. It uses OpenAI models, including GPT‑6 Astra and GPT‑Image‑2.5, to provide a fully guided workflow for video creation, including this post-apocalyptic adventure from a Pollo AI user.

Pollo AI reports that owners spend more than 50% less time choosing or switching models, giving them more time for creativity.

In a recent development, pollo AI tests generative models against real user prompts and workflows, evaluating output quality, consistency, stylistic range, speed, and cost. GPT‑Image‑2.5 was selected to handle image generation, helping creators make posters, storyboards, and campaign visuals.

Pollo AI’s primary consumers are content creators, and the platform is especially popular for creating micro dramas with both AI and human actors. However, more marketers and business owners are starting to use Pollo AI to develop video content swiftly and easily too.

The finished image created a playful scene the brand could use in its campaign.

Across recruiting, engineering, and operations, Oracle turns specialist knowledge into fast, repeatable workflows with ChatGPT Work and Codex.

Decrease in the time it takes for talent acquisition research.

Over a hundred thousand employees across Oracle are using ChatGPT Work and Codex, from talent acquisition to Oracle Applications Lab to the IT organization. In each case, work that used to rely on specialists and take days can now be done by anyone and is complete in minutes. Recruiters skip days of market research, business people describe an outcome instead of hunting for a report, and technical leads build tools that used to take a full team months.

The talent acquisition team used ChatGPT Work to build a talent market intelligence tool that takes a job description, researches comparable roles, benchmarks compensation, and assesses the talent pool across relevant locations. The tool arms the recruiter with valuable information that they need going into a conversation with the hiring manager, information that previously took 2–4 days to compile.

According to recent reports, “We’ve gone from zero to a hundred,” says Jan Ackerman, Senior Vice President and Global Head of Talent Acquisition at Oracle. “Now we’re able to sit down and prep for about 15 to 20 minutes using the tool that we’ve built using [ChatGPT] Work.”.

Sources indicate that not only is the process faster, but it’s also more consistent. Recruiters used to run the intake process differently from one search to the next, but with the talent market intelligence tool, the process is consistent, so every hiring manager has the same quality of data and insights, no matter which recruiter they worked with.

Recent findings suggest that the Oracle Applications Lab team, which helps run many of Oracle’s core business processes, built an ontology of the company’s objects, relationships, and rules, so a plain-language business question can be turned into a reliable SQL query with Codex. A business user describes the outcome they want, and Codex decides which internal systems to call, gathers the information, and returns an analysis, a report, or an application.

That’s a change from how work used to get done. Lam remarked one user came to him after asking a question that would normally have taken her a couple of hours to answer. She told Lam, “With the upcoming tool, I put in the request and got a response almost immediately.” When she checked the result against the old manual process, the numbers matched exactly.

According to recent reports, in production engineering, site reliability engineers use Codex to gather relevant context about an incident and automatically pull up the right playbook. SREs spend more time guiding decisions and less time hunting for information. “A typical simple incident that used to take an hour to resolve can now be handled in minutes,” notes Lam.

Even as Codex takes on more of the work, Lam is careful to note that none of this runs on autopilot. Someone still has to make sure the underlying system is built right.

While AI builds the tools, the people are still responsible for the output. A few lessons stand out:.

Recent findings suggest that give the correct guardrails. “You have to still be very responsible about your system design, your architecture, your security, and how you would like Codex to structure the code for you,” indicates Lam.

Sources indicate that provide prototypes instead of specs. “Normally, I put [my idea] down on paper, but now I put it down in a prototype,” indicates Barry Shilmover, Vice President and Technical Advisor to the CIO.

Recent findings suggest that own the code. “If you don’t work alongside Codex, you’re going to get into a situation of having lots of code that is not going to be maintainable,” says Lam.

The Oracle team is completely shifting how the manufacturer operates with AI. Across recruiting, analytics, and engineering, each line of business described an outcome and let Codex and ChatGPT handle how the work gets done. With thousands of ChatGPT and Codex consumers already, Oracle employees use AI across countless work tasks. As Shilmover puts it, “I don’t know what the answer is because I don’t know what my next problem to solve will be. I just know that one of the first things I’ll do is I’ll leverage Codex to do that.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Using GPT‑6 Astra in Codex, Asana made its browser agent 76x cheaper and 5x faster in tests to offer customers more capable models.
  • Lower estimated model costs with the optimized GPT-6.1 Sol workflow.
  • Faster browser runs with the optimized GPT-6.1 Sol workflow.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Using GPT‑6 Astra in Codex, Asana made its browser agent 76x cheaper and 5x faster in tests to offer customers more capable models.

Lower estimated model costs with the optimized GPT-6.1 Sol workflow.

Faster browser runs with the optimized GPT-6.1 Sol workflow.

Average estimated model cost with the optimized GPT-6.1 Sol workflow.

With GPT‑6 Astra in Codex running experiments, Asana optimized its browser agent’s workflow on GPT‑6.1 Sol to run 76x cheaper and 5x faster.

In a recent development, asana helps customers automate work across business applications through StackAI⁠(opens in a latest window), a platform it acquired⁠(opens in a new window). Using StackAI, customers can build workflows that navigate websites, fill out forms, and gather information without writing code. At Asana’s scale, small inefficiencies in these workflows add up.

Recent findings suggest that asana’s StackAI CTO, Frank Hidalgo, PhD, set out to make the browser agent faster and cheaper to run. He directed GPT‑6 Astra in Codex to investigate the agent, test improvements, and compare the results. Work he estimates would have taken one to two months by hand took about a week.

Asana’s 144-run study⁠(opens in a latest window) tested GPT‑6.1 Sol and three other frontier models, called here Models A, B and C. The optimized workflow that emerged on GPT‑6.1 Sol averaged $0.47 in estimated model costs and about four minutes per run, 76x cheaper and 5x faster than the original production setup on Model B.

To move quickly, Hidalgo started by using GPT‑6 Astra in Codex to map the codebase and explain how the agent built each model request. GPT‑6 Astra discovered that the agent cached its fixed instructions and tool definitions, but not the growing history of page text and screenshots it gathered, so every request resent that history at full price.

The agent also dropped older screenshots and trimmed text at nearly every step. Each edit altered the history, so caching the history alone would not have helped, and losing those facts could require the agent to revisit pages it had already read.

Hidalgo reviewed GPT‑6 Astra’s proposed fixes and selected three to test:.

Extending caching to the agent’s browsing history.

Increasing the amount of text it could retain.

Removing screenshots in batches rather than at every step.

It has been revealed that GPT‑6 Astra began with quick tests to establish which variables mattered. Because the code was not designed for controlled experiments, it then refactored the code so one frontend and backend could support many workflows in parallel, each with its own settings.

Recent findings suggest that astra conducted the full study: history budgets of 120,000 and 480,000 characters and six caching and screenshot policies, each tested three times on each of the four models (see the table below). The best-performing policy allowed screenshots to accumulate to 20 before cutting back to the most recent one. This kept earlier history unchanged for longer stretches between removals. Combined with the larger history budget, it became the optimized workflow. Each configuration performed the same task: collecting six fields for each of 32 books from a public demo catalog, representative of what some Asana customers run in StackAI.

A smaller, less expensive model from another frontier lab, released Fall 2025.

The model originally used in production, from the same lab as Model A, released Summer 2026.

An updated version of Model B, released Fall 2026.

GPT‑6 Astra ran the workflows and examined the requests, usage records and outputs, and separate model sessions reviewed the work. Every session’s requests, data traces and results were recorded in Command⁠(opens in a new window), Asana’s software delivery platform, so the team could review the complete study afterward. From Command, the findings were turned into tickets, then pull requests, and the changes went to production.

For Model B, the optimization reduced estimated model cost from at least $36.21 (some original runs reached the step limit before they finished) to $1.24 per run, a reduction of 29x. The optimized workflow on GPT‑6.1 Sol was 2.6x cheaper still, at $0.47. Every run in the optimized workflow completed the task and returned the correct answer.

Means of 3 runs. ≥: the baseline includes capped runs, so its mean is a lower bound.

Industry observers note that the two right folds compare against Model B optimized. Model B ran in phase 1, Model C and Sol 6.1 in phase 2 of the same study (dotted line).

On GPT‑6.1 Sol alone, with the larger history budget, the new caching and screenshot policy reduced cost 4x, from $1.97 to $0.47 per run. Each call was about 3x cheaper, because 89% of the input came from cache at 5% of the uncached price. Runs also became faster: at least 22.5 minutes on the original setup on Model B, roughly four minutes with the optimized workflow on GPT‑6.1 Sol.

Mean of 3 runs, SD whiskers. ≥: mean includes a capped or unfinished run, so the true value is at least this large.

Bars use the blue theme. Read caching effects against the 480k larger-budget bar.

Sources indicate that bars use the blue theme. Read caching effects against the 480k larger-budget bar.

Run markers and SD whiskers are approximate reconstructions from the source image; underlying run values and standard deviations were not available.

Sources indicate that the investigation also revealed how history management affected whether the agent produced an answer at all. Giving GPT‑6.1 Sol more room to retain its browsing history increased the number of runs that produced an answer from three of 18 with the smaller history budget to all 18 with the larger budget, each with the correct answer. For Hidalgo, the business value is giving customers access to faster, more capable models while keeping operating costs sustainable.

Industry observers note that asana has released the changes to browser navigation in StackAI and is developing tools to make similar experiments easier to repeat. Over time, the team looks to incorporate this testing into the platform’s evaluations, so customers and internal teams can compare cost, runtime, and answer quality when configuring their agents.

Recent findings suggest that asana is now using GPT‑6 Astra in Codex to test product features before release: Astra navigates the platform, tries different inputs and reports bugs for human QA reviewers. Hidalgo views this as the foundation for a new software development lifecycle, with many cloud agent sessions testing features in parallel.

The complete study is available on the Asana⁠(opens in a upcoming window) and StackAI⁠(opens in a new window) blogs.

Tech Report: Sophos cuts threat investigation time by 96% with OpenAI Daybreak

📅 09 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (793 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • With OpenAI Daybreak, Sophos combines frontier intelligence with cybersecurity expertise to investigate threats faster and protect customers at scale.
  • reduction in investigation time using OpenAI models.
  • Frontier AI is changing cybersecurity on both sides⁠(opens in a latest window).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With OpenAI Daybreak, Sophos combines frontier intelligence with cybersecurity expertise to investigate threats faster and protect customers at scale.

average response time for cases using AI agents.

reduction in investigation time using OpenAI models.

of MDR cases resolved end-to-end by AI.

Frontier AI is changing cybersecurity on both sides⁠(opens in a latest window). Advanced models can help defenders find and investigate threats faster. But those capabilities are also spreading to open-weight models, giving attackers new ways to discover vulnerabilities and accelerate exploitation.

It has been revealed that sophos⁠(opens in a newly introduced window) is one of the companies standing in their way, protecting more than 625,000 organisations across sectors and regions. “We see a huge variety of different attacks,” indicates John Peterson, the firm’s Chief Technology Officer. “We’ve cultivated vast expertise in combating them over four decades in the cybersecurity business.”.

Industry observers note that through OpenAI Daybreak, Sophos is combining OpenAI models with its own threat intelligence, response playbooks and security expertise. The aim isn’t simply to give analysts another tool. It’s to increase the impact of Sophos’s expertise across every customer it protects.

“Sophos brings the domain expertise and the know-how to combat attacks at scale. Programmes like Daybreak, and companies like OpenAI, bring frontier intelligence that allows us to take that domain expertise and scale it to support all of our customers.”.

At the centre of the work is Sophos Fusion, the Sophos AI-native cyber defense system that includes Sophos Managed Detection and Response (MDR). It brings together sensor data from more than 500 third-party integrations alongside Sophos’s own products. Together, those sensors generate trillions of events every day, which Sophos distills into roughly 1,000 to 2,000 cases for its nine security operations centres to investigate.

Agents built through Daybreak have changed how those cases are handled. An investigation agent gathers the customer context, detections, indicators of compromise (IoCs) and relevant threat intelligence for each case. A planning model then creates a initiative–execute–review loop: building an investigation plan, completing the steps and producing a summary with recommended response actions for analysts to review. Other agents can carry out parts of the response.

Sources indicate that before Daybreak, investigating and responding to a case depended primarily on human expertise. Sophos’s existing process averaged around 38 minutes — performance Peterson says was better than 96% of professional security operations centres.

Recent findings suggest that “Now, because of the agents we’ve been able to build through the Daybreak programme, the average response time for cases using those agents has fallen to about 89 seconds. About half of the cases we handle are now being automated by agents we developed using the Daybreak models.”.

Sophos has built customer control into its MDR service through three operating modes:.

Notify: Sophos investigates the case and recommends a response, but the customer acts.

Collaborate: Sophos and the customer work together before action is taken.

Authorise: Sophos can respond directly on the customer’s behalf.

The same boundaries apply whether work is completed by a person or an agent. Sophos uses automation to move quickly and make better use of analysts’ time, but potentially destructive actions still require the right level of human oversight.

“Anything we don’t feel comfortable with an agent handling gets passed off for human judgement,” Peterson confirms.

Reduced the average response time for cases using agents from approximately 38 minutes to 89 seconds.

Enabled Sophos to resolve 52% of MDR cases end-to-end with AI, within boundaries calibrated by Sophos analysts.

Gives customers a faster and more consistent investigation experience.

Helps Sophos scale compute rather than relying on equivalent growth in scarce cybersecurity headcount.

Returns analysts’ attention to the threats, exceptions and decisions where their expertise matters most.

It has been revealed that peterson indicates Sophos will keep expanding what its agents can do. “The response capabilities are going to continue to become more sophisticated, and we’re going to broaden the range of use cases we address with the agents we’ve built.”.

“With programmes like Daybreak, we have an opportunity to stay a step ahead of the attacker community.”.

In a recent development, his advice for other security leaders is simple: “The one thing security leaders should do tomorrow is really come back to focusing on the security fundamentals for their organization,” he says. “That of course includes patching. But patches are only ever going to include vulnerabilities that are known by the vendor.”.

In a recent development, the answer is to maintain “a layered security approach” that includes endpoint protection, multifactor authentication (MFA), network segmentation and strong security operations. “Vulnerabilities are being discovered at an alarming rate and exploited at a scale that we’ve never seen. So I think doing the fundamentals well is more notable today than it’s ever been.”.

For Higgsfield AI, the ambition is to make creating a film feel more like describing an idea, with AI handling more of the work in between.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, across the EU, businesses are expanding how they use AI through agentic tools. People are moving beyond asking questions to using agents to carry out tasks from planning through completion. Our latest report from OpenAI Economic Research examines how agentic use is growing across enterprises and small businesses, focusing on differences in usage intensity and the kinds of work people do with ChatGPT.

We have found that, among ChatGPT Enterprise customers, agentic use already represents a substantial share of activity⁠. In our EU sample, Codex and ChatGPT Work now account for more than half of output tokens.

This analysis defines small or medium businesses as businesses with 200 or fewer associated customers.

Industry observers note that the agentic shift extends to small and medium businesses. Since May 2026, weekly active customers of Codex and ChatGPT Work among EU small and medium businesses grew more than eightfold, with growth across every member state.

In a recent development, but we also found that the EU’s adoption of agentic AI is far from uniform. Among the ChatGPT Enterprise accounts in our sample, the share of output tokens generated through Codex and ChatGPT Work ranged from 22% in Slovenia to 85% in Lithuania. The differences across countries extends beyond the intensity of agentic use. The kinds of work people bring to ChatGPT also vary across countries.

Industry observers note that frontier firms are defined as the top 10% of firms by output tokens per active user. Sample includes only ChatGPT Enterprise and Business accounts.

Sources indicate that the takeaway is that EU frontier firms use AI much more intensively than typical EU firms, but still trail firms at the global frontier. In September, frontier firms in the EU generated more than four times as many output tokens per active user as typical EU firms. Even so, frontier firms outside the EU generated more than twice as many output tokens per active user as frontier EU firms. EU-based firms also represented only 10% of the frontier firms globally, which is low considering that the EU accounts for a higher share of registered companies globally⁠(opens in a new window).

Sources indicate that these figures reveal a substantial gap in how intensively businesses use AI. As agentic capabilities advance, the EU’s opportunity is to turn broader adoption into deeper use, stronger businesses, higher productivity and meaningful benefits for workers. Closing that gap means helping businesses move beyond experimentation, giving workers the skills and confidence to use AI, and making advanced capabilities more accessible and affordable.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Block is using AI systems including OpenAI Daybreak to compress the time to fix vulnerabilities, freeing its security team to focus on strategic work.
  • Hour to replay a proposed detection change against seven months of telemetry.
  • Minutes from submitting a high-level vulnerability to an automated proposed patch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Block is using AI systems including OpenAI Daybreak to compress the time to fix vulnerabilities, freeing its security team to focus on strategic work.

Hour to replay a proposed detection change against seven months of telemetry.

Minutes from submitting a high-level vulnerability to an automated proposed patch.

Analyst-hours per quarter handed back.

Analyst-hours of investigation completed each quarter.

At Block, the company behind Square, Cash App, and Afterpay, the security team leverages the OpenAI Defense Factory: where AI handles vulnerability discovery, detection, and response at a scale that no human team could keep up with. With AI systems including OpenAI Daybreak, Block is taking just hours to do work that used to take weeks.

In a recent development, block’s security team has been focused on responsibly adopting AI across workflows, whether that’s code generation or security operations. “What it’s really centered on is having a latest teammate that you can scale with,” James Nettesheim, Chief Information Security Officer, says. “It’s not like a more traditional automation where you had to go step by step. You can prompt it with a fairly bespoke, ambiguous problem and work through it together.”.

According to recent reports, projects like reviewing a software bug or parsing a log would take days or weeks to complete. Now the team can complete those projects in a fraction of the time, with a human still validating every result.

In a recent development, for example, for detection tuning, every investigation stores its raw query evidence, so the team can now replay a proposed detection change against seven months of production telemetry in under an hour. That work used to mean requerying hundreds of old cases by hand, and often it rarely happened in practice since it was so time-consuming.

In a recent development, the team has also gotten more particular about which model they’re using for which job. “We used to use the latest model, but you don’t need to do that anymore,” he indicates. “It’s been a learning experience to choose different models for different tasks.” Block’s security harness is built on top of Daybreak to help route tasks to the right model, and it includes hooks for humans to take over tasks or for agents to verify each other’s work. The team continually evaluates these systems against internal benchmarks and real-world performance, adjusting its approach when needed, including routing work to human review when that is the responsible path.

Recent findings suggest that the automated triage system has resulted in faster work (and more of it) getting done. Block’s security team has seen a 50% boost to triage throughput, a 50% increase in intelligence gathering and investigations, and an entirely newly introduced autonomous hunting capability. Nettesheim indicates, “This performs ~1,100 analyst-hours of investigation per quarter, because every alert now gets a full, deep investigation across all elements the alert involves. Our system works every alert like it’s the only alert we’ve got that day.”.

Recent findings suggest that traditional scanning tools flag a single vulnerability in isolation, but Block’s security team can go much further with Daybreak. The model helps hypothesize about attack patterns and chain together a series of attacks into a full end-to-end compromise path, surfacing vulnerabilities that might have existed for years.

In one case, an alert on a single laptop looked like a minor policy glitch on its own. But during peer review, the model followed an indicator that appeared only incidentally in the evidence, joined it against Block’s identity logs, and surfaced a much larger set of concerns. “One routine endpoint alert became a campaign takedown. No single tool makes that join. The signal only exists across two products’ logs,” James states.

Another example when Daybreak helped was during a recent red team exercise. The model was given a few hints about an internal system, and it chained together a full attack path—SQL injection, privilege escalation, a foothold, credential enumeration, and a pivot to other systems—in about two hours. This would typically take a human red teamer several days. In recent red team exercises, the time from submitting a high-level vulnerability to an automated proposed patch was 18 minutes.

Finding the vulnerabilities is only as good as the ability to fix them. Nettesheim walks through the process his team uses on every finding: locate where the concern lives in the code and identify who owns it, then move to remediation. “You propose a patch, you confirm exploitability, and then you verify that you have fixed it, with a human in the loop guiding it and deploying the code changes.”.

While agents are technically capable, they don’t carry an organization’s context or the reasoning behind previous decisions. A human provides that context and strategy, and that’s where his team comes in to provide a human layer of review. As AI’s judgment is proven out in practice, Nettesheim indicates, “we’ll slowly ladder up the risk level to use it for more sensitive systems.”.

Less than one hour to replay a proposed detection change against seven months of telemetry.

18 minutes from submitting a high-level vulnerability to an automated proposed patch in recent red team exercises.

Roughly 600 analyst-hours per quarter of false-positive triage handed back.

Approximately 1,100 analyst-hours of investigation completed per quarter.

50% boost to triage throughput.

50% increase in intelligence gathering and investigations.

Recent findings suggest that detection and response work alone has handed back roughly 600 analyst-hours per quarter that used to go toward triaging false positives. With that time back, the team now spends more time on deeper investigations and building more automation responsibly.

As the pace of attack increases and AI models keep advancing, Nettesheim sees an opportunity to reduce the number of vulnerabilities introduced in the first place. That would free security teams to spend less time patching and more time on preventative, strategic work.

Sources indicate that “OpenAI is shifting the advantage to defenders by putting these advanced capabilities in everyone’s hands,” he indicates. “It’s typically only been in very high-profile technology companies and government hands. But everyone, including critical infrastructure, schools, small businesses, can now start utilizing this technology to defend their networks.”.

How Third Moment Research runs 10,000 agents for 36+ hours

📅 14 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1081 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • With GPT‑6 Astra and GPT‑6.1 Sol, Codex, and Daybreak for cybersecurity, this AI lab builds agents that focus for days and improve with use.
  • Industry observers note that every organization has its own workflows, tools, edge cases, and definitions of success.
  • The tech giant is building a self-improving AI system around that idea, using OpenAI’s latest models to understand agent behavior, identify recurring weaknesses, and automatically create thousands of synthetic scenarios around those problems.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With GPT‑6 Astra and GPT‑6.1 Sol, Codex, and Daybreak for cybersecurity, this AI lab builds agents that focus for days and improve with use.

Hours per autonomous research session.

Reduction in backtest time with Codex.

Trillion OpenAI tokens in a single day.

Industry observers note that every organization has its own workflows, tools, edge cases, and definitions of success. ⁠(opens in a fresh window)Third Moment Research⁠(opens in a new window) believes the best agents should be really good at that specific work and should improve their capabilities the more they’re used.

The tech giant is building a self-improving AI system around that idea, using OpenAI’s latest models to understand agent behavior, identify recurring weaknesses, and automatically create thousands of synthetic scenarios around those problems. The team uses those scenarios to improve agents, repeating the process as latest issues emerge.

In a recent development, codex, GPT‑6 Astra, GPT‑6 Sol, and GPT‑6.1 Sol support the system’s research and computational work, enabling Third Moment to run 10,000 agents at once on investigations lasting 36-48 hours. The organization also uses Daybreak to test the security of the environments where agents work.

One of Third Moment’s early applications is in the field of quantitative finance given the clear measure of success. This domain provides a concrete setting to study how agents work and where they struggle. The team uses Codex to find and address problems in the research environment.

In one instance, it used Codex with GPT‑5.6, the latest GPT model at the time, to analyze thousands of recorded simulation trajectories (the agents’ actions and the environment’s responses) alongside timestamps and the codebase.

Codex uncovered a bottleneck: backtesting a trading strategy across a year of order-level US equity data took several hours. While waiting, agents repeatedly polled for completion, wasting tokens and filling their context with status checks.

Sources indicate that after profiling the backtest and analyzing its inputs and usage, Codex identified a caching optimization and a memory-packing technique. It experimented with solutions and deployed the fix to production, reducing the backtest from approximately 3 hours to approximately 3 to 5 minutes. This reduced token use and context pollution, freeing more of the agents’ token budget for further experiments.

Industry observers note that third Moment gives each agent the tools, information, and environment it needs for a specific job. For quantitative research, the team runs the default Codex harness inside a Dockerized environment. Agents receive a terabyte of data, documentation, and a research repository with modules for feature engineering, GPU-supported model training, trading strategies, and simulation.

GPT‑6 Astra, GPT‑6 Sol, and GPT‑6.1 Sol provide the reasoning, while the Codex harness gives agents tools to act, create plans, set objectives, spawn subagents, and compact context as work continues.

To address agents that stop before completing a task, Third Moment treats Codex as a subagent within an outer harness powered by GPT‑6 Sol or GPT‑6.1 Sol. The outer harness examines the trajectory when a task is left unfinished and determines whether to retry, terminate the job, or escalate to human review.

In that research environment, agents work to improve a baseline trading system built by Third Moment’s engineers. They test trading strategies on historical data, assess whether an improvement is meaningful or noise, and use each result to choose the next experiment. According to Adam, their work has improved the baseline trading system.

According to recent reports, before GPT‑5.5, Adam claims models could only execute experiments prescribed by a user. With GPT‑5.5 and GPT‑5.6, models working with the Codex harness could use results to design follow-up experiments. Now with GPT‑6 Astra, GPT‑6 Sol, and GPT‑6.1 Sol, agents can investigate root causes through hundreds of experiments running in parallel with subagents.

It has been revealed that that progression has helped agents explore research directions the team hadn’t anticipated. In one session, GPT‑6.1 Sol identified the impact of non-displayed trades on an exchange where those trades accounted for an unexpectedly large share of volume. “This was an unobvious result that our research team did not initially consider,” says Adam.

It has been revealed that third Moment evaluates models across optimization, machine learning systems, and quantitative research. It tests frontier releases at their highest reasoning settings, assessing their ability to navigate repositories, write efficient code, and sustain an investigation. Current testing also includes GPT‑6 Luna.

It has been revealed that one benchmark asks agents to reduce a live scoreboard service’s update latency while preserving its outputs. The team measures speedup by dividing the average runtime of an expert-crafted solution by that of the model’s solution on the same hardware, subject to correctness. GPT‑6 Astra delivered the biggest speedup, according to Adam.

For targeted work, including checks for specific security weaknesses in the simulation system, the team uses more efficient models like GPT‑5.6 Terra. For deep research, Adam believes stronger reasoning can justify higher cost: “In the space of quantitative finance, the value of finding some interesting signal is extremely high.”.

With 10,000 agents running autonomously, Third Moment needs a way to test the security of its research environments at scale. The team uses the Daybreak cybersecurity platform to automate that testing before simulations launch.

In a recent development, the tests check whether an agent could break out of its research environment and access the wider network. “By using Daybreak, we’re able to have agents themselves do penetration testing on the simulation and test the infrastructure and security of it,” claims Adam.

In a recent development, third Moment’s ambition extends to the specialized work companies do every day. For a retailer, that could mean making better supply chain decisions when inventory is short or a supplier is delayed. For an engineering team, it could mean finding performance bottlenecks in a large codebase. For a document-heavy business, it could mean identifying where commitments in one document don’t match outcomes recorded in another.

Recent findings suggest that building on the reasoning capabilities of GPT‑6 Astra, GPT‑6 Sol, and GPT‑6.1 Sol, Third Moment plans to expand from individual investigations to hundreds of thousands of collaborating subagents. Its roadmap calls for trillions of tokens supporting chains of dozens of dependent experiments, with the goal of using that research to autonomously improve agents as newly introduced challenges arise.

For Adam, this would give people more capacity to shape how agents learn and work: “Humans can be in a much more leveraged position, where they can think about how to do research and optimize the research itself instead of actually doing the research.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • With OpenAI Daybreak, SentinelOne cuts weeks of malware analysis to hours, creating capacity to investigate more threats.
  • Hours to reverse-engineer malware, down from 4–6 weeks.
  • Reverse engineering a sophisticated piece of malware can take a top security researcher four to six weeks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With OpenAI Daybreak, SentinelOne cuts weeks of malware analysis to hours, creating capacity to investigate more threats.

Hours to reverse-engineer malware, down from 4–6 weeks.

Reverse engineering a sophisticated piece of malware can take a top security researcher four to six weeks. It’s painstaking work where researchers pull apart software to understand how it behaves, often retracing their steps as they uncover fresh information. Gregor Stewart, Chief AI Officer at SentinelOne, states OpenAI Daybreak can now produce human-level reverse-engineering output in roughly eight hours.

By reducing the time needed for deep analysis, OpenAI gives SentinelOne’s researchers room to investigate more malware and connect findings across samples. That wider view often reveals relationships that isolated investigations might miss. Stewart describes the opportunity as “a kind of intelligence that we were never able to afford before.”.

Daybreak gives defenders access to OpenAI models for cybersecurity work. SentinelOne uses these capabilities to reverse engineer malware, examining software to understand how it behaves. Faster analysis gives its researchers more capacity to investigate additional samples.

According to recent reports, stewart emphasizes that his team remains responsible for the outcome. “The only thing that can’t be automated is accountability,” he says. “Take a decision to change the architecture. This is something that still you would want human eyes on, whereas point fixes or things that don’t fundamentally change the way the software works, those might be better suited for automation,” he adds.

Industry observers note that historically, research teams at SentinelOne had to reserve deep investigation for the most interesting or important threats they uncovered. “We were only able to reverse very small numbers of pieces of software,” Stewart states. With fewer samples to compare, they had fewer opportunities to spot connections between threats.

It has been revealed that faster analysis with Daybreak gives researchers more opportunities to compare malware samples and look for shared components. For example, a component found in two apparently unrelated samples could give researchers a lead to pursue during a customer investigation.

According to recent reports, comparing findings across more samples also reveals broader relationships between threats. Seeing those relationships, Stewart notes, “would help you defend further out, and be more proactive about your defense.”.

According to recent reports, within SentinelOne, Stewart says access to OpenAI’s cyber capabilities is allowing more people to take responsibility for security work. “Almost everyone now has access to the kind of expertise that was in very short supply until maybe even a few months ago,” he says. More team members can investigate complications themselves rather than relying on a small group of specialists.

Stewart wants to bring OpenAI’s cyber capabilities into code creation, so SentinelOne developers can address security challenges as they build.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

See how Amp pushes the frontier of what agents can do with GPT‑6 Astra, Ultrafast, GPT‑Live‑1, and Sign in with ChatGPT.

Amp⁠(opens in a new window) is building a frontier AI agent that helps developers turn ambitious ideas into working software. For Quinn Slack, Amp’s CEO, each improvement in the models is an opportunity to expand what the agent can do, from helping developers decide what to build to writing code and designing pages.

Sources indicate that amp chooses and recommends models based on what works best for its users, and OpenAI models account for the majority of tokens used in Amp. Quinn shares, “OpenAI is very transparent, and when there are safeguards applied, users know and they understand. That makes it really easy to use OpenAI models. You can do all of your work in Amp with OpenAI models and be really happy.”.

As builders give agents more work, token costs can become a constraint. Quinn describes some Amp consumers consuming 10 billion tokens a week. He believes that if people watch every increment of usage, it might hold them back from finding out what an agent is capable of.

To help alleviate that, Amp launched its Sign in with ChatGPT integration. Quinn claims it gives Amp users access to more tokens and OpenAI models, including GPT‑6 Astra, which changes how willing they are to let an agent take on a larger task.

Sources indicate that “Sign in with ChatGPT means that people can have that feeling where they’re not counting every single token,” he indicates. “And once you actually let the agent go and have a longer leash, then you realize just how much it can do.” Quinn says he sees people using the agent to proposal, decide what to build, and continue working after they ship.

Industry observers note that amp wants agents to help with all the work that goes into building and growing a product. Its own 20-person team uses them that way, including in marketing. “We don’t have someone devoted to it, but we have an agent devoted to it,” Quinn says. The team relies on the agent to improve the experience for latest people and help more people discover Amp through search and other channels.

Sources indicate that for that work, having high-quality writing and design is critical. GPT‑6 Astra helps the team produce documentation and design pages that meet Amp’s exacting standards.

Quinn’s experiments with GPT‑6 Astra continue at home. He gave it the plans for his house and used it to create a 3D model in Blender. He and his children then turn that model into games: adding a lazy river through the house or chasing garlic around it, inspired by their grandmother’s dislike of garlic. “And that was not possible just a couple months ago,” he claims.

Industry observers note that amp recently declared Puck, a conversational AI assistant built into Amp that helps owners launch and manage other agents. Users can ask Puck to start an agent to investigate a bug, coordinate several agents, or find a previous conversation about a technical problem.

Industry observers note that with Calling Puck, powered by GPT‑Live‑1, users can talk to Puck in real time, including from a watch. Quinn imagines people using it to keep their agents working while they’re away from their computers, even while out for a run.

Amp has been testing Ultrafast mode with GPT‑6 Astra, and Quinn claims the greater speed changes how people use agents. Today, people often switch between several agent tasks while waiting for each to finish. Faster responses could let people juggle fewer agents, or give agents more time to check their own work before returning a result.

For Amp, the next step is to bring more of the work before and after coding into the agent, so builders can carry an idea further without handling every step themselves. “There’s this unknown of what humans will create, and that’s what we all get to see. It’s cool to be playing a part in that,” Quinn notes.

Sullivan & Cromwell brings legal expertise into agreement review

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In collaboration with OpenAI, Sullivan & Cromwell developed Agreement Analyzer, an AI tool for identifying issues in a draft agreement.
  • Sources indicate that for lawyers at Sullivan & Cromwell, reviewing a draft agreement includes weighing its terms against relevant precedents, using approaches based on the Firm’s experience and being mindful of a client’s priorities.
  • Though AI was initially used most for repetitive, administrative tasks like drafting email responses or checking calendars, Savva finds that recent improvements in AI models’ analytical capabilities have changed its usage.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In collaboration with OpenAI, Sullivan & Cromwell developed Agreement Analyzer, an AI tool for identifying issues in a draft agreement.

Sources indicate that for lawyers at Sullivan & Cromwell, reviewing a draft agreement includes weighing its terms against relevant precedents, using approaches based on the Firm’s experience and being mindful of a client’s priorities. The firm’s Agreement Analyzer brings those inputs into a single review workflow, producing analysis and proposed changes that lawyers can inspect and refine.

Though AI was initially used most for repetitive, administrative tasks like drafting email responses or checking calendars, Savva finds that recent improvements in AI models’ analytical capabilities have changed its usage. “Now, we’re seeing many more opportunities for use in challenging legal tasks such as deep analysis of complex agreements,” he indicates.

Agreement Analyzer helps lawyers compare corresponding provisions across precedents and track how those provisions interact.

It has been revealed that sullivan & Cromwell partner John Savva developed Agreement Analyzer as a single-user proof of concept built with Codex. He then collaborated with OpenAI on improving the quality of outputs, enhancing efficiency through parallel processing and transforming the application into a tool that could be used by multiple lawyers at the same time.

Agreement Analyzer integrates Sullivan & Cromwell’s workflows, curated firm precedents, negotiating playbooks and ChatGPT Enterprise. After inputting a draft agreement into the tool, a lawyer can add their own selected precedents and a playbook with firm and client positions, as well as information on market practice. The tool performs multiple review cycles from different perspectives, synthesizes the outputs, helps identify potential concerns and returns a memorandum and proposed tracked changes for a lawyer to review, adapt or reject.

Savva emphasizes that what makes an AI tool’s output trustworthy is full transparency. “If an AI tool makes a claim about market practice, you need to be able to see the source of that information,” he notes.

Savva describes an application in which agents develop conclusions and other agents challenge them in an adversarial process. In a potential use case, specialized agents review the agreement in parallel for such things as market deviations and risk allocation, interactions between clauses, and ambiguities that could impact litigation. The results distinguish findings supported after challenge by other agents, dismissed findings, and unverified issues retained with qualifications. Lawyers can inspect the issues, their supporting explanations, and the relevant precedents, then decide which findings warrant changes in the final markup.

In a recent development, sullivan & Cromwell is continuing to explore tools shaped around specific legal tasks. For Savva, stronger analytical capabilities create an opportunity to support more of the research and writing process.

Savva points to advances in reasoning capabilities with GPT‑6 Astra: “Astra’s really moved things forward in terms of the quality of the reasoning that’s available, and that has been the bottleneck in the past,” he claims.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • On Teachers’ Day, we celebrate those who help us learn.
  • Set in a university classroom, the campaign takes a humorous look at the changing relationship between teachers and students and celebrates the role of educators in a world with AI.
  • Sources indicate that today, we are launching the AI for Educators⁠(opens in a new window) course in Brazilian Portuguese on OpenAI Academy, OpenAI’s free learning platform.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On Teachers’ Day, we celebrate those who help us learn. A good question can change the course of a lesson. It can bring an unspoken question to light, open up another way to solve a problem, or help someone recognize what they already know. Teachers do this work every day: they know their students, choose how to introduce an idea, and guide them from their first attempt to understanding.

Set in a university classroom, the campaign takes a humorous look at the changing relationship between teachers and students and celebrates the role of educators in a world with AI.

Sources indicate that today, we are launching the AI for Educators⁠(opens in a new window) course in Brazilian Portuguese on OpenAI Academy, OpenAI’s free learning platform. Designed for educators in primary, secondary, and higher education, the course shows how to use AI to proposal lessons, create activities and assessments, and prepare communications while preserving educators’ pedagogical judgment.

It has been revealed that study Mode helps you explore a subject⁠(opens in a fresh window) step by step, with questions, hints, explanations, and checks for understanding. Developed in collaboration with teachers, scientists, and experts in pedagogy, the feature aims to encourage active participation and reflection on one’s own reasoning.

To turn on Study Mode, select Study from the tools menu in ChatGPT.

A student reviewing biology, for example, might ask: “I’m studying enzymes. Ask me one question at a time, wait for my answer, and help me identify what I need to review.”.

Teachers can also try Study Mode with subjects they know well, looking at whether the questions encourage reasoning and whether the explanations are appropriate for their class.

In a science lesson on evaporation, for example, a teacher might ask students to investigate why clothes dry on a clothesline. After exploring the topic with Study Mode, each student writes their own explanation and a question to discuss in class, without referring back to the conversation. The teacher can use these responses to identify what needs to be revisited with the class.

This Teachers’ Day, we invite you to experiment: explore the AI for Educators course, try Study Mode, and discover how these tools can be useful in different teaching contexts. Technology can open up fresh ways to learn, but it is teachers who know their students, ask the most important questions, and help turn curiosity into knowledge.

Introducing the Rosalind Academic Plan, offering eligible labs sponsored access to GPT‑Rosalind and tools for life sciences discovery.

Recent findings suggest that we’re introducing the Rosalind Academic Plan to help more academic scientists access GPT‑Rosalind⁠, our dedicated life sciences model, which combines frontier reasoning with Rosalind workbench⁠(opens in a latest window) that enables specialized tool orchestration across medicinal chemistry, genomics, wet-lab assistance, and other scientific applications. Eligible labs can receive up to 30 Business Standard seats at no cost for up to 12 months, with access to GPT‑Rosalind subject to trusted-access approval.

Recent findings suggest that academic research creates knowledge that entire fields build on. Work that begins with a fundamental question about biology can eventually change how we diagnose disease, develop medicines, or grow food. But those advances depend on scientists having the resources to explore ideas, test them, and share what they learn.

In a recent development, accelerating scientific discovery is central to OpenAI’s mission of ensuring that artificial general intelligence benefits all of humanity. With this proposal, we’re investing in the scientists doing that foundational work—helping more labs combine their expertise and judgment with AI tools built for life sciences research.

Many of the advances we rely on today grew out of years of basic research.

The Human Genome Project helped launch modern genomics, transforming medicine, diagnostics, and biotechnology.

Industry observers note that curiosity-driven work on bacterial immune systems led to CRISPR-Cas9, which revolutionized genome editing and is now advancing research in cancer, inherited disease, agriculture, and biotechnology. Decades of university research on mRNA also laid the groundwork for COVID-19 vaccines and a newly introduced generation of vaccines and therapies.

Sources indicate that academic research has always laid the groundwork for advances in medicine and biotechnology. By helping more scientists combine their scientific expertise and judgment with the advanced specialized reasoning of GPT‑Rosalind, we hope to support discoveries whose benefits reach far beyond the lab.

According to recent reports, openAI is committed to enabling academic researchers to pursue their scientific ambitions. Distinguished academic labs are already exploring how GPT‑Rosalind can support work ranging from protein design to understanding neurodegeneration. These examples show where researchers are applying the model within their scientific workflows.

With the new Rosalind Academic Blueprint, academic researchers can bring GPT‑Rosalind and Rosalind Workbench to their lab with greater flexibility and harness frontier model intelligence for scientific research.

In a recent development, GPT‑Rosalind is a specialized life sciences model designed to support deeper reasoning on complex biological questions. Through trusted access, approved researchers can use it to investigate sensitive scientific questions within safeguards designed for legitimate research.

Designing candidate drugs, therapeutic proteins, peptides, and enzymes, and optimizing their molecular interactions, selectivity, stability, and suitability for development.

Identifying molecular signatures of disease and developing liquid biopsies and other minimally invasive diagnostics to detect disease earlier, monitor progression, and assess treatment response.

Designing and evaluating antibodies and vaccines against emerging viral variants, investigating host–pathogen interactions, and studying the strength and durability of protective immune responses.

Developing approaches to correcting genetic defects and modulating gene expression, designing RNA therapeutics, and investigating how to deliver treatments safely and effectively to intended tissues.

Investigating crop resilience, plant disease, and animal health, and applying genetic, nutritional, and biological insights to improve food production and veterinary care.

Studying biodiversity, adaptation, species interactions, and environmental exposures to understand ecosystem change and inform conservation, bioremediation, and responses to climate change.

Studying how microorganisms resist antibiotics, antivirals, and antifungals, and developing new treatments for resistant infections, biofilms, and persistent disease.

The Rosalind Academic Plan is right now available to academic labs at U.S. universities. We’re starting with academic labs as part of a broader effort to put useful AI tools in the hands of more scientists. By lowering the cost of access, we hope to give more researchers room to pursue ideas whose benefits could reach far beyond their own labs—from a clearer understanding of disease to better treatments and more resilient food systems.

Those advances will come from scientists asking important questions and doing the work to answer them. We want to help more of them do that work.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Two engineers shipped Stack Overflow for Agents in a few weeks with Codex, and its ChatGPT plugin helped drive up to 10× growth in agent creation.
  • More signups for Stack Overflow for Agents overnight with the ChatGPT plugin.
  • Maximum reduction in time to build one connector, from 3–6 weeks to 4 days.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Two engineers shipped Stack Overflow for Agents in a few weeks with Codex, and its ChatGPT plugin helped drive up to 10× growth in agent creation.

More agents created with the ChatGPT plugin.

More signups for Stack Overflow for Agents overnight with the ChatGPT plugin.

Maximum reduction in time to build one connector, from 3–6 weeks to 4 days.

According to recent reports, people and AI agents need context to get work done, but it’s usually scattered across systems, from Slack to Google Docs. Finding it and understanding how it all fits together can be a challenge.

That’s why Stack Overflow⁠(opens in a new window) is building a knowledge intelligence platform that unifies those sources and turns raw context into verified knowledge available wherever people and agents work.

According to recent reports, openAI models like GPT‑6 Astra and GPT‑6 Sol power the platform’s AI, with tasks routing to different models based on the reasoning required and cost. Codex helps the company’s engineers build the products, while a ChatGPT plugin makes their newer agentic product, Stack Overflow for Agents, easier to discover and use.

Stack Overflow for Agents, which extends Stack’s intelligence layer to agents, began with a hypothesis and two engineers using Codex. The engineers gave Codex a development environment and a plan, and then worked with it to build the product. Within a few weeks, Alex notes, they had a full-fledged product.

“So it really made their team feel bigger,” Alex says. “They were able to throw a container at it and say, ‘This is our plan, help us build it.’”.

Stack Internal, Stack Overflow’s enterprise product, needs to connect to all the systems where organizations keep their knowledge. Building this capability requires more human involvement than the two-engineer effort behind Stack Overflow for Agents, but Codex is accelerating this work, too.

Sources indicate that alex describes using Codex to pursue a much shorter path to market for the enterprise product: three months rather than a year. Building connectors is one concrete example.

More recently, the team built a connector in a single day. By accelerating connectors, Codex helps Stack Overflow bring enterprise products to market faster.

Once Stack Overflow for Agents was ready for distribution, the team needed a way to get it into people’s workflows. It built a ChatGPT plugin so users could discover and set up the product in ChatGPT, with fewer steps than a traditional Model Context Protocol (MCP) setup.

Alex notes the plugin tripled registrations and accelerated agent creation: “I think we were up to 10X last time I checked.”.

Stack Overflow manages its own model routing and configuration, but Alex hopes to explore using the Decisions API to reduce some of that work and put more engineering capacity into the product.

“If we’re able to automate that through OpenAI directly, that saves us a ton of time and money, allows us to focus more on the actual product we’re building rather than the guardrails around it,” Alex indicates.

Stack Overflow is also working on expanding its knowledge product to enable sharing of what people learn. To date, its focus has been pulling information in. Now, Alex is closing the loop so knowledge gained in a one-to-one session with a developer or someone outside engineering can help others, too.

It has been revealed that “As I’m learning, how do I make sure that the rest of my organization is learning with me?”, said Alex. “I’m really looking forward to building a product that allows for that full knowledge life cycle.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Anant Kumar builds tools to compare loan valuations and analyze credit agreements, using Codex for code review and faster follow-ups.

First BDC mark tracker version; ~10–12 total development hours, including refinements.

First-pass credit agreement analysis, followed by 1+ hour of human review.

It has been revealed that at Benefit Street Partners, a credit-focused investment manager, answering an investment committee’s follow-up questions used to take days or weeks. Portfolio manager Anant Kumar says analysts can now turn a round of comments in a day with Codex, and often answer questions during the meeting itself. BSP is using these tools to add more review capacity and rigor to underwriting within the same timeframe, rather than to do more deals.

To create a dashboard he could share with colleagues, Kumar used to need someone with software expertise to build a website and pull in the data. Now he builds his own tools, using AI to draft code and review it for errors.

His tracker uses public SEC filings from business development companies (BDCs) to compare how firms value the same loan. The team can see how its marks compare with other holders’ valuations.

Kumar built the tracker and used Codex for code review. The first version took a day. After adding features and refining the interface over subsequent weeks, he estimates total development time at 10–12 hours total.

It has been revealed that kumar’s other tool analyzes credit agreements, which are often 300 pages or longer. Investors need to find clauses that could shift value away from lenders, a task that previously meant asking outside counsel to work through the agreement page by page. Kumar brought together memos from leading law firms on clauses and risks to watch for. He describes the analyzer as a “second brain within our organization.”.

An uploaded credit agreement takes about 20 minutes to process into a first-pass analysis, followed by an hour or more of human review. BSP has refactored the tool with GPT‑6 Astra, and it is now live in the company-hosted portal.

“The AI is very helpful in collating data, ingesting it, synthesizing analysis, but the ultimate investment decision needs to be made by a human,” he says.

Underwriting is typically a multi-round process. A round consists of further diligence and a revised memo responding to the investment committee’s questions. Deal timelines range from a few days to a few weeks, so the number of rounds varies. Kumar says, “We feel more confident in our decision making because we have more information at our disposal.”.

Built the first BDC tracker in a day, using Codex for code review; about 10–12 hours total including later additions.

Produces a first-pass analysis of a credit agreement in about 20 minutes, followed by an hour or more of human review.

Answers committee follow-up questions faster with Codex, often during the meeting, according to Kumar.

BSP is working to connect information across deals. Continuous underwriting is a longer-term aspiration: the team could monitor loans as news happens and examine the effects across its portfolio, rather than re-underwriting only after an event.

“Codex has unlocked my day, because I have many more hours in the day to do more high-level work and less routine work,” states Kumar.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that for the tech giant, generative AI is more than a productivity layer: it is a newly introduced computing interface. That commitment takes shape across three areas—transforming the business, creating new customer interfaces, and building AI-native products.

When generative AI arrived, Localiza took a view that defined everything that followed: this was more than another piece of software in the toolkit; it was a change in the way the company operates.

In a recent development, rather than pursuing isolated use cases, the company organized its collaboration with OpenAI around three strategic pillars: transforming the business through experimentation at scale, creating latest customer interfaces, and building AI-native products. What connects all three is the decision to redesign processes around intelligence, context, and speed.

The principle guiding internal adoption is straightforward: scale enables learning, and learning creates better products.

In practice, that meant distributing ChatGPT licenses as a resource for experimentation and productivity, rather than simply as an individual benefit. Teams across Localiza, from finance to day-to-day operations, maintain active experiments with custom GPTs, agents, and Codex.

It has been revealed that codex first arrived in the technology department—software engineers, product managers, designers, and data scientists. But adoption did not stop there: analysts, managers, PMOs, lawyers, and other business specialists began building their own prototypes and automations to test hypotheses within their areas of expertise.

This was an effect the tech giant had not anticipated—a redefinition of the stages before development, with multidisciplinary teams prototyping solutions before they enter a development queue.

The bottleneck, he states, is human rather than technical.

The second area starts with an observation about behavior: people have begun describing what they need in natural language, creating a latest entry point for mobility services—at the very moment they express their intent.

Localiza’s internal data confirms this shift: traffic originating from LLMs has been growing rapidly since 2024, with ChatGPT emerging as the main channel.

In a recent development, the company chose to establish a presence in this space early. In March 2026, it became Brazil’s first mobility platform—and one of the first in Latin America—to offer an app integrated directly into ChatGPT. Customers can explore rental, subscription, and used-car options and begin their journey in the conversation, before completing the transaction in Localiza’s secure environment.

Internally, Localiza’s app in ChatGPT is treated as what it is: an experiment designed to keep the organization close to the frontier of customer behavior, accelerate learning from real interactions, and explore how AI complements the existing ecosystem.

The manufacturer’s clearest example of an AI-native product is Liza, a conversational assistant that has become an established success story in its operations.

The difference from a traditional chatbot lies in the architecture, not the interface. Rather than following a fixed decision tree, Liza was built around conversation, intent, and context: it combines OpenAI models, Localiza services, and specialized tools to support key parts of the experience, from understanding the initial request to assisting with key stages of the rental journey.

The ambition is to handle repetitive journeys with quality and free teams for complex, higher-value interactions.

But success is not measured by the volume of automation.

Localiza was already mapping and measuring its customer service journeys before it had access to this type of technology—and that foundation made it possible to decide clearly where an agent should step in and where a human needs to intervene.

It has been revealed that liza also serves as a continuous learning loop: aggregated, monitored signals from interactions help identify needs, points of friction, and service opportunities. Combined with voice capabilities—voice-to-text and text-to-voice—these signals support its evolution from a transactional chatbot into an AI-native customer interface that can learn and scale across different mobility journeys.

The partnership with OpenAI began early: the first version of Liza still ran on GPT‑3.5.

For Petenussi, the central value of the relationship lies in active learning between two companies evolving in parallel, rather than in a specific feature—with the partner understanding Localiza’s challenges and the different maturity levels of its capabilities, both within and outside technology.

It is an argument he often makes to other companies in the market: with a technology that is still maturing, trial and error and close collaboration have considerable value.

In March 2026, Localiza became the first organization in Brazil, and one of the first in Latin America, to launch an app integrated directly into ChatGPT; more recently, it joined the platform’s advertising pilot in Brazil as an advertiser.

Traffic from LLMs has been growing rapidly since 2024, with ChatGPT as the main channel.

The Liza assistant operates with more than 60 specialized agents, built on reasoning models, MCP integration, and specialized tools that orchestrate the rental journey.

Teams across the firm—from finance to operations—maintain active experiments with custom GPTs, agents, and Codex.

Codex reached the technology department and spread to business areas, with analysts, managers, PMOs, and lawyers building their own prototypes and automations.

The technology operation is organized into 19 tribes and 130 squads.

Industry observers note that treat AI as a new operating model, rather than a productivity layer. The greatest gains come from redesigning processes around intelligence, context, and speed.

Sources indicate that use scale to generate learning. Simultaneous experiments at scale produce more organizational knowledge than a perfect pilot.

Take experimentation beyond technology. When lawyers, PMOs, and analysts prototype within their own areas, the nature of upstream work changes.

Industry observers note that map and measure your journeys before automating them. Having quality metrics in place enables you to decide where an agent should intervene and where a human is indispensable.

In a recent development, the adoption bottleneck is reskilling, not the model. Changing how hundreds of people work is harder—and more decisive—than integrating the technology.

Start with the customer’s problem and journey, rather than a model feature.

Allocate licenses as an experimentation budget, rather than an individual benefit.

Establish quality metrics before scaling conversational agents.

Treat a presence in new conversational channels as a learning experiment, rather than an acquisition campaign.

Close the loop: use the signals generated by each interaction to improve the product itself.

Localiza’s ambition is to put AI at the center of its next experiences and processes—whether in how work is produced, the experience created for customers, or the resolution of an operational problem.

The next areas already being developed with OpenAI include the evolution of Liza and sales-focused agents, the establishment of conversational interfaces as a customer entry point, and the new cycle of agentic software development.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Almost 50 years after starting in a compounding pharmacy in Paraná, the group operates a proprietary agent platform that autonomously resolves up to 80% of resellers’ operational requests—enabling the sales force to take on an advisory role.

autonomous resolution of operational requests.

of conversations generated in appchat and WhatsApp Enterprise covered since November 2025.
