📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

From local businesses to global brands, more advertisers can now reach people as they explore, compare and decide what to buy in ChatGPT.

Industry observers note that more than 1.2 billion people use ChatGPT each week to explore ideas, compare options and make decisions. Ads can help people discover products and services that fit their needs, including options they might not have found otherwise.

Since we released ads just over eight months ago, over 100,000 advertisers have run campaigns on ChatGPT. Today, we’re expanding ChatGPT Ads to 26 additional countries, extending availability to 89 countries worldwide. This launch builds on our recent expansions across Europe and Southeast Asia and Taiwan.

Industry observers note that advertising helps support free and low-cost access to ChatGPT for people around the world. Our mission is to ensure that artificial general intelligence benefits all of humanity. Ads will appear only on the Free and Go plans. Plus, Pro, and Enterprise subscriptions will remain ad-free.

Following our releases in Mexico and Brazil, we’re bringing ChatGPT Ads to 14 more Latin American countries, including Argentina, Chile, Colombia, and Peru. We’re also launching in more markets across Europe, the Middle East, Africa, and Asia, including Nigeria, South Africa, Serbia, Ukraine, Cambodia, Bangladesh, and Pakistan.

Advertisers can access ChatGPT Ads in these countries through technology partners or self-service access through Ads Manager⁠(opens in a latest window).

In ChatGPT, people can explain what they’re looking for, ask follow-up questions, and refine their options through conversation. Someone training for their first marathon might start by exploring meal ideas for race week, then narrow their options based on their dietary preferences and how much time they have to cook. An ad relevant to that conversation could introduce them to a grocery delivery service they hadn’t considered.

For local businesses, regional brands, and international companies, ChatGPT Ads gives businesses a way to introduce their products during these moments of consideration, when people are still evaluating their options and deciding what’s right for them.

Protecting the trust people place in ChatGPT is foundational to our approach to advertising.

Guided by OpenAI’s ads principles, we keep conversations private from advertisers and do not sell customer data. Ads in ChatGPT are clearly labeled and separate from ChatGPT’s answers, and advertising does not influence the answers ChatGPT provides.

Our goal is to make ads useful to people as they pursue their goals and make decisions—and effective for the businesses that advertise with us.

Our focus remains expanding access to AI while staying true to our principles.

Sources indicate that with ChatGPT Ads now available in 89 countries, our next phase of growth will include the development of additional formats, objectives, buying options, and measurement capabilities. We are also continuing to explore new ways for businesses to interact with consumers in more native ways in ChatGPT.

As more people turn to ChatGPT to explore needs, evaluate options, and make decisions, we see an opportunity to help them discover products and services—and to help businesses of every size grow and thrive.

Businesses interested in advertising on ChatGPT can learn more at ads.openai.com⁠(opens in a newly introduced window).

Patch the Planet: global response coordination as agents uncover critical vulnerabilities

📅 21 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1891 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that over the past two months, we led a coalition of maintainers, researchers, and security providers to address critical vulnerabilities in PHP, an open-source programming language used to run websites and web applications.
  • For organizations using PHP, the priority now is applying the fixes.
  • Given the severity of these flaws and PHP’s widespread use, we consider this one of the most impactful security concerns in recent memory.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that over the past two months, we led a coalition of maintainers, researchers, and security providers to address critical vulnerabilities in PHP, an open-source programming language used to run websites and web applications. Calif identified a critical flaw using GPT‑5.6 Sol as part of our Patch the Planet⁠(opens in a newly introduced window) initiative, with Wiz also independently discovering and reporting both vulnerabilities. PHP’s maintainers led the fixes and release, with our teams and partners like Wiz, Cloudflare, and others contributing research, technical support, and coordination to prepare protections ahead of disclosure.

For organizations using PHP, the priority now is applying the fixes. We’re sharing a PHP version checker as a Codex skill⁠(opens in a new window) to help operators identify potentially vulnerable PHP versions and, alongside PHP’s and their providers’ guidance, determine which updates apply.

Given the severity of these flaws and PHP’s widespread use, we consider this one of the most impactful security concerns in recent memory. It highlights how AI can uncover security flaws with internet-scale impact, but the same capabilities can also help attackers rapidly develop offensive tools and exploits.

To our knowledge, frontier AI found these vulnerabilities before attackers did, opening a Defender’s Window for maintainers and security providers to prepare fixes and protections ahead of disclosure.

To help more defenders use these capabilities, we’ve committed $1 billion in subsidized Daybreak access through Daybreak for Frontline Defenders, focused on organizations with limited security resources protecting essential services.

As significant as they are, these bugs are among several significant vulnerabilities we’ve already found and are working to fix, and we expect similar findings to increase sharply in the coming months. Drawing on our experience thus far, we’re sharing a proposed approach, appropriate for the AI era, to responding to critical vulnerabilities in widely used software, and we’re asking the security community to help improve this framework. It brings together our models, security expertise, and maintainers to help turn findings into protection and build a response that can scale as AI capabilities advance.

Sources indicate that getting a fix into use can mean adapting it for older releases, preparing provider mitigations, and updating systems across many organizations. A repeatable process helps those teams act quickly as more vulnerabilities are discovered.

Through Patch the Planet, we contributed security expertise and model access to support the PHP response, and worked with maintainers and research partners to test fixes and prepare guidance. We also helped coordinate with infrastructure providers on protections for affected systems and engaged government cyber agencies to help guidance reach critical organizations. This supported the maintainer-led response and helped other defenders prepare.

For some findings, researchers can work directly with the software’s maintainers to investigate the issue and develop a fix. Others need a wider response because they affect many products or because distributors and service providers need time (which may be in short supply if frontier capabilities are not too far ahead of those that are broadly available) to prepare updates and protections. In those cases, the proposed framework can help maintainers identify who needs to be involved and coordinate the work. The response can involve five stages:.

Sources indicate that validate and fix the upstream vulnerability. The maintainer, researchers, and essential technical partners confirm the finding, assess its impact, and develop and test a fix. This process includes adversarial testing with frontier models to look for ways around the patch and related variants of the vulnerability.

It has been revealed that give affected organizations time to act. We propose a framework for considering which organizations need advance information to prepare protections, while maintainers decide whom to involve. We help with outreach, information-sharing agreements, and coordination between teams. A distributor might adapt a fix for an older release, a hosting provider might test a mitigation, and a security provider might prepare detection or prevention measures, including web application firewall (WAF) rules.

Coordinate with government partners to help protect critical systems. Government agencies play an essential role in coordinating a wider response and helping security guidance reach organizations responsible for critical infrastructure and other essential services. In the case of PHP, we worked, in collaboration with our partners, to engage with multiple parts of the U.S. government, including the White House’s Super Intelligence Force, the Office of the National Cyber Director (ONCD), the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), as well as international partners to support that effort.

In a recent development, prepare updates across affected products. As the fix, guidance, and disclosure plans become stable, maintainers can involve additional distributors, hosting and service providers, response teams, and operators to prepare updates and address gaps in coverage.

In a recent development, once a patch is available, publish guidance and support deployment. Public guidance helps people assess their exposure, find authoritative updates or interim mitigations, and check that a fix is running. The response continues as operators deploy updates and report where they need help.

The proposed framework considers an organization’s protective role, including protecting its own systems and customers, the time needed to act, and its ability to handle sensitive information. The same criteria would apply to comparable organizations, with maintainers deciding whom to involve ahead of disclosure.

Sources indicate that each participant receives the information needed to carry out their protective work, from network logs with indicators of compromise to more sensitive working proof-of-concept exploits. Even limited details can reveal a vulnerability, so we weigh the risk of sharing them against the protection they enable.

Teams following this framework would work with maintainers to give defenders time to prepare and reassess the timeline if there’s active exploitation in the wild, a leak, a revealing public patch, or increased risk to customers from stalled remediation.

The Patch the Planet website⁠(opens in a upcoming window) brings together public disclosures and guidance to help operators identify affected systems, find the right update, and verify that the updated software is running properly. For PHP, it points to the maintainers’ official patch and upgrade instructions and our partners’ technical research. The guidance also covers interim mitigations, when to involve a provider or expert, and backup and recovery. Interim protections can reduce risk, but we’ll make their limits and operational tradeoffs clear.

In a recent development, operators can use CISA’s guidance on prioritization and remediation⁠(opens in a newly introduced window) to assess how swiftly to act based on exposure, exploitation, and potential impact. That may mean emergency patching, immediate mitigation, or a planned patch, alongside forensic triage where warranted to assess whether systems have already been compromised. Priorities should be reassessed as conditions change, with a clear path to lasting remediation.

Global coordination depends on the people who maintain the software. Many projects are run by small teams that review security reports alongside routine development. Those teams need help separating new issues from duplicates, assessing impact, and testing fixes across supported releases. We support that work with funding, access to capable models, and hands-on engineering help.

Recent findings suggest that powerful AI capabilities are advancing across the industry, and we expect AI to play a growing role in helping defenders find vulnerabilities, monitor systems, and respond to threats. We’re investing in models, tools, and partnerships to help defenders put those capabilities to work.

In a recent development, our investments include subscriptions for all maintainers through Codex for OSS and direct sponsorship of projects such as the Rust Foundation⁠(opens in a upcoming window) for maintainers and technical work. Each project sets its own priorities. Reusable tests and security workflows can reduce the effort needed to handle future findings. Open-source projects can apply to Patch the Planet⁠(opens in a new window) for hands-on support.

Industry observers note that we’re also calibrating additional blocking classifiers for Daybreak to help reduce the potential for misuse. This involves difficult tradeoffs: safeguards intended to prevent abuse can also block legitimate security work. Broad access to capable models and effective protections against misuse are both critical. Our aim is to preserve the capabilities defenders need to find and fix vulnerabilities while limiting harmful use. We’ll continue refining that balance as capabilities advance and we learn from how these tools are used.

Recent findings suggest that as models become more capable, the opportunity extends beyond finding and fixing individual vulnerabilities. We want to help engineers build more secure software from the start. Improvements to a widely used component can prevent bugs or limit their impact across many products and services.

It has been revealed that AI can help engineers understand existing code, prepare changes, and develop tests, while maintainers and security experts verify that those changes preserve the behavior users depend on. We see opportunities in several areas:.

Sources indicate that secure code from the start. Coding models can help developers choose safer defaults, use security libraries correctly, and catch risky patterns as they write. Preventing vulnerabilities during development means fewer emergency fixes for maintainers and owners.

Sources indicate that memory-safe software. Moving critical components to memory-safe languages can eliminate common classes of memory errors. AI can help with migrations, with tests and expert review to check behavior and compatibility.

Formal verification. Mathematical proofs can show that critical components satisfy specified security properties under stated assumptions. Applying these methods to widely used components could help rule out classes of vulnerabilities across the services and critical infrastructure that depend on them.

In a recent development, stronger isolation. Systems need protection against vulnerabilities that have not yet been found or fixed. Running software that processes untrusted files, images, or media in tightly restricted sandboxes can limit the damage if it is compromised. AI can help engineers test and strengthen widely used sandboxing technologies, improving protections across many applications.

Sources indicate that we’re sharing our approach so maintainers, researchers, response teams, providers, and operators can help make it workable. We want to understand where it would help, where it could add delay or burden, and what we’ve missed. Examples from past disclosures would be especially useful.

We’re particularly interested in:.

Sources indicate that disclosure windows. How much time do maintainers, operators, and defenders need to prepare and deploy reliable fixes? What evidence should trigger earlier disclosure, especially when some users can be protected sooner than others?

Sources indicate that emergency patching. When, if ever, should governments or other operators use a vulnerability to patch systems they own or are authorized to manage after losing administrative access? What safeguards should apply? We can imagine an end-state of internet-wide always-on scanning for known vulnerabilities, and either notifying site owners when one is detected or patching the system.

Early notice. Who needs advance warning to take a useful protective action, including defenders we might miss? When do staged notifications work better than notifying a wider group at once, and how should we weigh coverage against leak risk?

Recent findings suggest that secure-by-default software packages. How can we help identify and fix vulnerabilities in downstream packages while upstream fixes are pending, or backport fixes to older versions that no longer receive security updates? What testing and maintenance would make these packages reliable options when a timely upgrade isn’t feasible?

In a recent development, we also welcome recommendations for independent security experts who can review the approach, challenge its assumptions, and identify gaps. Your input will help us refine the response and prioritize support. Share your feedback here⁠(opens in a new window).

Sources indicate that openAI and Google Cloud⁠(opens in a upcoming window) are partnering to bring OpenAI’s frontier models and Codex⁠(opens in a new window) agentic workflows into Google Cloud’s Model Garden. The integration will give customers native access to these models to power complex agentic workflows at scale, backed by Google Cloud’s data governance and high-performance infrastructure.

According to recent reports, google Cloud’s longstanding investment in machine learning and AI has made it a destination for AI workloads and the developers and data scientists building them. Bringing OpenAI models to its model garden gives these teams access to OpenAI’s frontier models within the environment where they already work, enabling enterprises to modernize their software development lifecycle, build agentic workflows, and change how people work.

Industry observers note that for organizations in regulated industries, deploying AI requires control over who can access sensitive data and how it is used. The integration will pair OpenAI’s frontier models with Google Cloud’s built-in access controls, centralized data governance, and high-performance infrastructure to support demanding enterprise workloads.

Google Cloud customers will be able to purchase OpenAI frontier models via model garden, transacted through the Google Cloud Marketplace. Enterprises with Google Cloud spend commitments will be able to draw down their GCP commitments for these purchases.

It has been revealed that additionally, OpenAI models will soon be available in Google Antigravity and the Gemini Agent, providing enterprise customers with model choice flexibility and the best model for each task. By expanding access through Google Cloud, we are giving enterprises greater choice in how they discover and use frontier models, with a path from evaluation to broader adoption.

Industry observers note that general availability is planned in the coming weeks. Request access to OpenAI on Google Cloud here.

Microsoft remains OpenAI’s primary cloud partner.

Breaking: Broad access through consistent standards

📅 21 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (631 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Over the past few months, we’ve worked with customers and partners to align safety policies across services that provide our models.
  • Recent findings suggest that models such as GPT‑6 Astra expand what developers and businesses can build.
  • In a recent development, before deploying a model, we evaluate its capabilities and risks, train it to follow safety requirements, and test whether its safeguards hold up when people deliberately try to bypass them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Over the past few months, we’ve worked with customers and partners to align safety policies across services that provide our models. We’re also updating our Usage Policies to make those requirements clearer and easier for developers to follow.

Recent findings suggest that models such as GPT‑6 Astra expand what developers and businesses can build. As those capabilities grow, we’re working to keep safeguards effective and consistently applied across the services that offer our models.

In a recent development, before deploying a model, we evaluate its capabilities and risks, train it to follow safety requirements, and test whether its safeguards hold up when people deliberately try to bypass them. As we describe in our approach to safety and alignment, we combine safeguards designed to reinforce one another.

Sources indicate that after deployment, we monitor for potential abuse and investigate concerns. To mitigate cyber misuse, for example, we train models to refuse harmful requests and use systems that look for suspicious patterns across interactions to decide how to respond. Trusted access programs provide another layer of protection and set eligibility requirements and conditions for access to our most powerful capabilities.

Industry observers note that some safeguards are built into the model and others depend on the systems and people around it. Both need to be effective whether people access our models directly or through a partner.

It has been revealed that developers and businesses should be able to choose where they access our models, with consistent safeguards across those services. We developed policies to align our safeguards across providers and are working with each of our partners to ensure their implementation meets or exceeds our safety standards. These policies apply whether people access our models directly through OpenAI, partners that host them, or through reseller partners.

These policies require partners that provide access to OpenAI models to maintain safeguards consistent with our own, investigate potential violations, and take appropriate action when concerns are identified. That includes coordinating on enforcement so that restrictions remain effective across services providing access to our models.

Sources indicate that putting this into practice means accounting for how different services work and how customers use them. Our work with customers and partners on Private Safety Processing is one example of how we can develop effective safeguards while giving customers greater choice and control over their sensitive data.

We’re also updating our Usage Policies, effective November 20, 2026, to clarify the rules for safe model development and sensitive uses of AI. The updated Usage Policies build on that work by requiring services that provide direct access to our models such as model routers or AI gateways to get our review and approval before offering that access.

We’ll keep explaining what’s allowed, what’s restricted, and how customers and partners can ask questions or resolve compliance concerns.

As our models become more capable, we’ll keep improving how we detect, investigate, and respond to misuse. Customers can face misuse through their end users, compromised accounts, or leaked API keys and we work with them to understand and address those problems.

We’re also working with customers to introduce SafetyIDs, which customers can provide to help us distinguish between individual end users in an investigation without OpenAI learning those users’ identities. With SafetyIDs, we can respond to potential misuse more precisely while reducing disruption to others.

We base enforcement decisions on documented conduct and risk, apply our rules consistently, and respond in proportion to the circumstances. When we restrict access, we revisit those restrictions if meaningful changes in conduct, commitments, or safeguards address the concerns behind our decision.

We want more people to benefit from AI. Clear rules and consistent safeguards should make it easier for developers and businesses to build, compete, and choose the services that work best for them.

How AT&T is rethinking in-house legal work with OpenAI

📅 21 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (389 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • AT&T is building on LegalEdge to explore new ways to support its legal team.
  • In a recent development, AT&T’s in-house legal department has hundreds of lawyers and legal professionals around the world.
  • AT&T is working with OpenAI to build that next phase.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AT&T is building on LegalEdge to explore new ways to support its legal team.

In a recent development, AT&T’s in-house legal department has hundreds of lawyers and legal professionals around the world. Before they can advise the business, they need to assemble facts, documents, and relevant past work, often drawing on expertise held across different teams. For David McAtee, AT&T’s Senior Executive Vice President and General Counsel, making that experience easier to access is central to how the department’s work can improve.

AT&T is working with OpenAI to build that next phase. “Our partnership with OpenAI is going to allow us to build that plumbing that powers the knowledge layer throughout the organization and that all of us will draw into,” McAtee claims.

It has been revealed that the collaboration builds on LegalEdge, AT&T’s team of attorneys, legal professionals, technologists, and project managers focused on applying AI to major legal matters. The next step is to connect more of the organization’s accumulated expertise to the work arriving on a lawyer’s desk.

Requests arrive from across the business, and legal teams need to respond promptly without overlooking risks. Before they can advise, they have to understand the concern, gather the relevant context and decide what needs attention first. That makes intake a critical part of protecting the business. Bill Ryan, AT&T’s Chief Compliance Officer, describes one planned initiative as an intake system with “a front door where we have natural language intake.” The system would classify and prioritize requests, connect them with relevant precedent, research, and past work, and give the responsible legal professional historical context and recommended first steps.

Sources indicate that that would give lawyers a more informed starting point, with less time spent gathering the material they need to assess a matter. Ryan sees the opportunity in helping the department bring its judgment to more of the business’s needs.

“What most excites me about the future is expanding our ability to provide legal judgment at greater scale,” he says.

For McAtee, the principle guiding that work remains clear: “The decision making will always remain with the lawyers.” The partnership’s goal is to put better information within reach so those lawyers can spend more time applying their expertise.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Uber announced the organization-wide rollout of ChatGPT Work, an agent that helps employees take on a wide range of tasks within ChatGPT Enterprise, starting today. The rollout will make ChatGPT Work available to more than 30,000 employees across Uber’s global workforce.

It has been revealed that expanding from an initial pilot of 1,000 employees, the rollout will give teams across Uber access to an agentic platform designed to take on complex, multi-step tasks and deliver finished work. The expansion makes ChatGPT Work Uber’s first organization-wide deployment of an agentic platform tailored for knowledge work.

ChatGPT Work connects with tools companies like Uber use on a daily basis, including Google Drive, Gmail, Google Calendar, and Slack, enabling workers to research information, prepare meeting briefs, create presentations, analyze data and complete workflows across applications.

ChatGPT Work also gives Uber access to OpenAI’s portfolio of frontier models. Uber will benefit from models like GPT‑6.1 Sol⁠ which will be deployed as the default capability within ChatGPT Work, balancing frontier performance and cost efficiency. Uber teams will also be supported by OpenAI multimodal capabilities, including voice and image generation, giving them the flexibility to choose the right models and tools for different needs.

The rollout will be supported by Uber’s internal AI skills library, approved integrations and dedicated employee training, helping teams across functions including operations, finance, marketing and product put the technology to work. Uber’s developers and software engineering teams will also continue using Codex to accelerate software development and streamline coding workflows.

Industry observers note that the expansion marks another step in Uber’s broader AI strategy and its collaboration with OpenAI. The companies plan to share further insights into adoption, use cases and measurable outcomes as the rollout progresses.

Industry News: What FDE means at OpenAI

📅 22 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1979 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • What we do, how we work, and how we solve enterprise’s toughest problems to deliver real impact.By: Colin Jarvis, Head of Forward Deployed Engineering at OpenAI.
  • When Codex came out, someone on the team asked me, “What do we do when Codex can just one-shot the use cases we spent the last few months building?”.
  • That question gets to the heart of what FDE means at OpenAI.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

What we do, how we work, and how we solve enterprise’s toughest problems to deliver real impact.By: Colin Jarvis, Head of Forward Deployed Engineering at OpenAI.

When Codex came out, someone on the team asked me, “What do we do when Codex can just one-shot the use cases we spent the last few months building?”.

That question gets to the heart of what FDE means at OpenAI. We work alongside customers to understand their hardest problems and build solutions they can depend on. What we learn helps shape our products and gives Research concrete problems to solve.

That is progress. If we make ourselves obsolete every couple of months, our FDE team is doing its job.

I founded the team in early 2025 to close what we call “the deployment gap”: the distance between what models appear capable of and what people can reliably use to do their work.

It has been revealed that model capabilities have moved faster than the systems and processes needed to put them to use. Sometimes the missing piece is a product. Sometimes a model performs well on a benchmark but cannot do the job with real-life variables and constraints.

Industry observers note that we focus on customers’ hardest problems. Where our models can do the job today, we work with Product and our customer to make the solution repeatable and, where they fall short, we work with customers and Research to define the gap and make improvements. Our goal is for each engagement to leave the next customer with a better starting point—if we raise the floor to the point our customers don’t need FDEs to solve this class of problem the next time, we have done our job well.

The challenge for John Deere, a 200 year-old agriculture business, was how to scale personalized advice for farmers.

One example is See & Spray, its precision weed-control technology, which uses cameras and machine learning to identify and spray weeds rather than treating entire fields to reduce chemical use by up to 70%.

But realizing those benefits depends on farmers knowing how to configure the technology, plan their season, and adjust their practices as conditions change.

John Deere deployed OpenAI’s APIs to help make that support personalized and scalable.

AI can answer farmers’ questions in natural language, provide tailored setup guidance and recommendations, identify when equipment may not be delivering its full potential, and help farmers understand the value they’re getting from the technology.

The opportunity extends beyond any single interaction: to deliver relevant guidance throughout the customer journey, helping farmers make better use of their equipment while improving efficiency and sustainability.

This is the kind of challenge OpenAI FDEs work to solve: helping organizations move from AI capabilities to systems that deliver practical value in complex, real-world environments.

Recent findings suggest that but the problems are often wide open, there may be no established ground truth, and there is no playbook. Everyone wants to build something that has never existed. Fewer people want to do what it takes to get there.

Finding talented FDEs while raising the baseline for “good enough” has meant constant experimentation and application.

At the start of every FDE team session, I put up a slide with one core value: “Start with the outcome, do what it takes to succeed, then follow with scale”.

An impressive demo can go a long way before anyone asks whether it works in the real world.

Our job is to solve the customer’s problem to a standard we can stand behind in production.

In mid-2025, we had around 15 FDEs working with a large semiconductor customer on 10+ use cases. The ambition was to make their verification process AI-native, covering:.

Root cause analysis and debugging.

Verification can account for ~70% of a project’s effort in this industry. The opportunity was enormous, and there were many possible places to start.

Some FDEs had joined OpenAI just days earlier and had never worked in semiconductors. They embedded with the customer’s verification team, studied chip design in their spare time, and built evals with the engineers to test whether the AI could generate useful tests and correctly diagnose chip failures.Alongside that learning, we built custom harnesses for the individual use cases. Over the first 3-6 months, all of them reached production and early user adoption. The payoff was seeing the metrics:.

~48% time saved through AI-based directed test generation.

22% median performance improvement through kernel optimisation.

Weeks of debugging compressed into hours.

When we played this all back the Chief Hardware Officer asked, “Did you guys work as chip designers before coming here?”.

Our FDEs don’t need to know the industry on day one but it is their responsibility to learn it.

It has been revealed that as coding assistants make software faster to build, understanding the customer’s business becomes even more crucial. We build teams with a mix of generalists and domain experts.

You need enough knowledge to make sound judgments, and enough curiosity to question assumptions about the status quo.

Sources indicate that in life sciences, for example, our FDEs’ scientific backgrounds help them earn trust with researchers working on pre-clinical drug discovery tasks such as target validation and prioritization, gene-expression analysis, and chemical synthesis-route reconstruction. That expertise lets them contribute informed judgment about how those workflows could improve.

According to recent reports, we had shown that these workflows could deliver value, but each still required too much custom integration to extend to another team. The next challenge was to preserve those results while making the software easier to deploy and maintain.

By then, Codex had grown in capability. One FDE tested rebuilding their application around it, then worked with the team to move the use cases onto a common harness with Codex at its core.

Custom applications became plugins and skills built on common Codex primitives. Codex also became the interface, allowing us to retire the separate terminal UIs and CLIs we had written for individual use cases.

We were able to remove roughly 90% of the custom code from each project, and this changed how we built, maintained and scaled these workflows:.

We could benefit from centralized improvements to Codex, reducing the amount of glue code required for each individual use case.

Industry observers note that key functionalities were bundled as skills and plugins, making them easier to share with each other and to be centrally controlled by the AI CoE. This meant that extending from one team to the next could be as simple as swapping in new connectors/MCP servers, building fresh evals (which we also had a skill for) and getting up and running.

Recent findings suggest that in one August 2026 example, the initial deployment took two months. Extending the solution to a second team took one day. The next teams onboarded faster as we scaled—this has continued, with a use case in August 2026 taking 1 day for the second team after the initial deployment took 2 months.

That is one version of making ourselves obsolete. The work we had done to reach production established what mattered. As the underlying product improved, we could replace much of our custom implementation and keep the value it delivered.

This is why the order matters. LLMs let us build fast. Use that speed to get something valuable into users’ hands, learn what holds up in practice, and then scale what works.

The same principle applies across all engagements.

OpenAI Presence, our product for enterprise voice and chat agents, grew out of real customer deployments. The work began with Swarm⁠(opens in a latest window) and evolved through the Agents API, and today one customer now handles more than half of its calls with AI.

In a recent development, getting those deployments into production taught us which problems needed a custom solution and which building blocks other teams could use. We brought those building blocks into Presence, making it easier for developers to automate regulated workflows without rebuilding the underlying infrastructure. Each deployment helped shape the product and gave the next customer a better starting point.

With Thrive Holdings, OpenAI FDEs and researchers worked alongside engineers and accountants to build Tax AI for Current’s accounting firms. During its pilot, Tax AI processed 7,000 tax returns and increased throughput by about 50%.

One of the hardest challenges was automating rental-property returns, which required six weeks of engineering and practitioner review to reach 90% precision and recall. The work created reusable patterns that made it easier to extend Tax AI to other complex tax schedules.

The teams are now applying the same approach to bookkeeping, audit, and IT support—building systems that improve through practitioner feedback and real-world use.

Sometimes a better product lets us simplify what we built but sometimes the model itself cannot yet do the job.

Recent findings suggest that if we only build what today’s models already make possible, we will not uncover the intelligence gaps Research needs to close next. Therefore a lot of our notable engagements start at those limits with the customer, FDE and Research committed to working through them together.

We had already developed a customer-service platform with a large telecommunications customer, and they wanted to extend it to voice.

Voice accounted for around 90% of their customer-service volume. These cases were more expensive to contain than chat, and brought a range of newly introduced technical challenges in getting accents, tone and latency/accuracy up to production grade. Getting it right would make a substantial difference to their business.

It has been revealed that during scoping, our model scored around 60% on the key evals we used to assess whether it could do the job in production. We had reached the limits of its capabilities. Function calling and instruction following in customer-service scenarios needed to improve.

In a recent development, we explained that to the customer and brought Research into the work. FDE worked with the customer to build the platform and define what the model needed to do. Research worked on closing the capability gaps, with successive model snapshots letting us test progress against the customer’s requirements.

Over six months, performance on the key evals rose from around 60% to 80% and then 90%+, reaching the levels needed for production.

The resulting voice model now supports that customer’s deployment, other custom customer-service deployments, and managed deployments through Presence. A problem encountered in one customer’s business helped identify improvements that could serve many others.

Each part mattered. The customer committed to working on a problem the model could not yet solve. FDE stayed close enough to frame that problem, build the platform and drive the engagement from start to finish. Research improved the underlying model capabilities.

This is the other version of making ourselves obsolete: helping turn a problem today’s models cannot solve into a capability future models can deliver. The return on our work extends beyond the hours we spend with any one customer.

In a recent development, I joined OpenAI to help make AI useful in people’s everyday work. That still guides the team. I often say to the team that in most cases in LLM development, Occam’s Razor applies—the simplest solution is the best. In a organization that is defined by its cutting edge research and in an industry that is tainted by hyperbole, we want to build stuff that works reliably which people in the field can depend on.

The goal is for each engagement to improve what comes next: a product that is easier to deploy, a model that can handle a harder task, or less custom work for the next customer.

Sources indicate that if you have a hard problem you want to solve, we’d love to work with you. If you want to help solve those problems, we’d love you to join us.

So what do we do when Codex can handle the work we spent months building?

#43765. RoboThink: Let the Agent Think, Let the Policy Act

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (341 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

RoboThink: Let the Agent Think, Let the Policy Act

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (341 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.30111v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Robot policies act in real time but fail without knowing why, whereas a reasoning agent that watches the robot can often tell what went wrong. Existing systems either hand the agent control, which takes minutes per episode, or let it send instructions. Yet a policy follows a new instruction only from a fresh start, since a half-finished task leaves it in states outside its training data. Nor can an instruction fix how the robot moves. If a drift keeps pulling the hand to the left, "push right, slightly" is not a task the policy has learned. We propose RoboThink, in which the agent thinks and the policy learns to act on the agent's guidance. An instruction channel tells the policy what to do. When the user states "the milk, not the butter" after the robot has started, the agent rewrites the instruction and the robot undoes its own motion, with no training. A feedback channel tells it how to move. It is taught from the agent alone with agent-labelled DAgger, role tokens and counterfactual feedback, and is read only by the policy's action module. On LIBERO, RoboThink with Claude Opus 5.5 raises success from 0.09 to 0.87 under an unknown constant drift and from 0.42 to 0.84 under a random one. It also completes misheard and changed requests in 0.91 to 1.00 of the episodes. Acting alone, GPT-6 Astra needs 2.1 min per success and over a million tokens per episode, whereas RoboThink needs 55 s and 8k tokens. The same recipe works across policies, for both vision-language-action models and world action models, and across robots, from one arm to two arms and a mobile manipulator. On all 50 RoboTwin 2.0 tasks with two arms, success rises from 0.12 to 0.74 under the constant drift and from 0.31 to 0.56 under the random one. Finally, the agent is a plug-in. A policy taught by one agent works with other agents, including open-weight ones, and grows stronger with a stronger agent, without retraining.

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (209 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

arXiv:2611.29750v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: For a producer of Hindi creative prose, drafting is cheap and editing is not: a machine-written episode, story, or essay reads as under-written and flat, laced with translationese, and it sometimes quietly alters what the source states. RASA-Bench targets that editing task across three Hindi prose forms, measuring how well a model refines an under-written AI draft, a task distinct from writing from scratch. Across 2,050 drafts and eight refiners (16,400 rewrites), a four-layer protocol credits a rewrite only after it passes a faithfulness check against its own source, then ranks the survivors by holistic editorial preference through per-form Bradley-Terry fits whose centered coefficients are standardized before equal-weight averaging. Staying faithful proves to be a decisive test that behaves differently by form: gate-failure rates range from 9.1% on short stories to 29.5% on audio fiction, and the drift that disqualifies a rewrite shifts from events and identity in narrative to claims and evidence in essays. A 600-case human audit puts gate agreement at 0.925 (0.91 to 0.94 across forms), whereas subjective preference is form-sensitive and least settled for essays, among human readers no less than the model judge. The benchmark, evaluation protocol, and Hindi prose diagnostics are available at https://abdur75648.github.io/rasa-bench.

Fixed or Deleted? External Feedback Lets Cheaper AI Coding Agents Repair Rule Violations

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (329 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

According to recent reports, arXiv:2611.29162v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Many defects violate project rules that the code itself does not reveal, such as layering constraints or required tests. We study whether LLM coding agents repair such violations better when an external checker reports them, with their location and a repair goal. Three models, a small, medium and large model, driven by an AI agent, worked on 25 pull requests with 31 planted defects in ten open-source projects, plus 5 correct controls, five times alone and five times with findings from CodeAssure (CA), a commercial checker. We also compare with GitHub Copilot code review, and compare CodeAssure's detection with nine free static-analysis tools run out of the box, including Semgrep and SonarQube Community. Counting a run as repaired only when the repaired code also compiles and keeps its feature, CA findings raised the repair rate from 26% to 69% for the smallest model, from 46% to 90% for the medium model and from 45% to 93% for the largest model (pull-request-level p < 0.001), and from 39% to 84% over all runs. Every Java, TypeScript and Python repair compiled. We found that agents often cleared a defect by deleting a newly added file. Metrics based on whether the defect is gone count feature deletion as a success. The largest model alone did so in 44 of 125 runs. CA includes a check for deleted files that largely prevents this. In an ablation with the check turned off, removals rose from 9 to 65 out of 375 runs and the repair rate fell to 54% (small), 70% (medium) and 85% (large model). The CA workflow also outperformed Copilot code review (p < 0.001). Together, the free tools detected 8 of the 31 defects, and CA detected all 31. With CA, the medium model repaired 90% of runs, against 45% for the largest model alone, at about one fifth of the mean cost per run ($0.17 against $0.91).

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Fast, focused, low-cost decisions for any application.
  • Applications and agents make many small decisions throughout a workflow: how to classify an input, where to route a request, or which action to take next.
  • Today, we’re making the Decisions API generally available.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Fast, focused, low-cost decisions for any application.

Applications and agents make many small decisions throughout a workflow: how to classify an input, where to route a request, or which action to take next. Individually, they are simple. At scale, their latency and cost add up.

Today, we’re making the Decisions API generally available. Built with GPT‑6 Luna, the Decisions API focuses Luna’s intelligence on questions with bounded answers, helping applications and agents make near real-time decisions from text, images, and structured inputs up to 10x faster than GPT‑6 Luna through the Responses API.

Recent findings suggest that since public beta, we’ve added a native GPT‑Live integration, prompt caching for reused context, and inference residency in the US and EU. Developers can also pass native JSON inputs, include images in question instructions, and ask up to 400 questions per request, twice the previous limit. We’ve also continued to improve latency, including additional capacity in several regions in Asia.

Early adoption of Decisions has shown its applicability across a variety of use cases.

Sources indicate that across OpenAI, teams are applying the Decisions API across product and business workflows. The dots team is using it to reduce response times and improve interactivity. Our Personal Finance team is using it to categorize transaction descriptions, while our Communications team is using Decisions to classify coverage by the themes and scores whether it reinforces or challenges key narratives—helping identify what warrants closer review.

These early examples show how fast, structured decision-making can turn incoming information into useful action across a wide range of use cases. Customers are applying the Decisions API just as broadly, from accurately attributing AI costs to making language-learning experiences more interactive.

Industry observers note that using the Decisions API is simple: developers define a question and its allowed answers, then provide context as text, images, or native JSON. The API returns one of three supported answer types—a probability, choice, or score—that applications can use to determine what happens next. The variety of answer types allows Decisions to be applicable across a wide variety of use cases. Decisions API supports three answer types:.

Estimate the probability that a condition is true, such as whether a product has visible damage.

probability: an estimate from 0 to 1 that the condition is true.

Select one of your predefined options, such as whether an agent should continue, retry, or ask for clarification.

choice: one of your supplied values. The response also includes probabilities and confidence.

Rate an input against ordered levels in a rubric, such as the severity of damage.

score: the probability-weighted average of the level indices.

Industry observers note that with GPT‑Live, you can bring natural, expressive conversation to your voice applications, with smooth interruption handling that keeps conversations flowing. Decisions API now integrates natively with GPT‑Live⁠(opens in a fresh window), helping applications make fast, focused decisions during live conversations. A customer support agent can decide whether to ask a clarifying question, route a request, or escalate an issue. An avatar can adjust its facial expressions as a user speaks to it, and based on the user’s words, respond with a wink or a smile to create a more interactive experience.

In robotic manipulation, a human video provides the context that specifies how a task should be performed. However, scaling human-video ICL on world-action models (WAMs) faces two challenges: task-level human-robot pairs are not temporally aligned with robot actions, and standard action losses allow policies to rely on initial-scene or task-identity shortcuts rather than tracking the context. We present Entangle, an in-context world-action model that maps a single human video and current robot observations to future visual states and executable actions. To scale temporally aligned training data, we convert recorded robot videos into matched human contexts via video-to-video generation, supplemented by real paired recordings. For model training, we combine variable-length video windows with an intra-task contrastive objective that distinguishes the paired action trajectory from other executions of the same task, preventing task-identity shortcuts. Without task-specific fine-tuning, Entangle improves steadily as aligned training data scales, reaching an average score of 83.5/100 across six unseen tasks on an Astribot S1 robot, and achieves a 69.5% average success rate on seven unseen RoboTwin tasks, outperforming Zero-WAM by 22.6 percentage points. Under Context-OOD, although trained only on scene-aligned pairs, Entangle transfers context-specified behaviors across rearranged layouts and substituted tools. Tech Report: SN-EDA: Skew-Normal Estimation of Distribution Algorithms

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (211 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

According to recent reports, arXiv:2611.26938v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Gaussian estimation of distribution algorithms (EDAs) converge prematurely on slopes, because truncation selection removes most of the variance along the gradient. The usual remedies enlarge the variance or shift the mean. We propose the skew-normal EDA (SN-EDA), which corrects the third moment instead. It samples from a skew-normal distribution whose skewness points along the cumulative path of the mean shifts, while the mean and covariance remain exactly the maximum-likelihood estimates. The estimation step is unchanged, and the skewness needs no control. On a linear function it raises the fraction of the variance that survives selection from 0.29 to 0.53. In a pre-registered test on 24 benchmark functions in 10, 20 and 40 dimensions the skewness, applied through a gate that the test finds dispensable, improves the Gaussian EDA significantly in five of six settings. When the population starts far from the optimum, the error, averaged logarithmically over a run, falls by one to three orders of magnitude, and the gain grows with the magnitude of the skewness as predicted. The skewness adds nothing to the anticipated mean shift, whose offspring distribution we show to be skewed already, and SN-EDA remains behind algorithms that also correct the second moment.

In a recent development, openAI and Poland’s NASK National Research Institute have signed an agreement to explore collaboration on AI safety, security and technical research. The partnership will bring together expertise from both organizations to better understand emerging risks, strengthen safeguards, and explore how advanced AI can contribute to a more secure and resilient digital ecosystem.

As AI systems become more capable, international collaboration between developers and public research institutions will be essential to understanding their risks and building stronger safeguards. OpenAI’s existing work with the US Center for Advancing Standards and Innovation for Super Intelligence (CAISSI), UK AI Security Institute (AISI) and other public research institutions around the world has already helped strengthen safeguards, identify and fix security vulnerabilities in AI agents, and advance frontier AI safety.

Through the agreement, NASK’s AI Safety Research Center – serving as the Polish Artificial Intelligence Safety Institute (AISI) – and OpenAI will collaborate on AI safety research, exploring ways to evaluate increasingly capable AI systems, identify potential vulnerabilities and strengthen safeguards.

Recent findings suggest that openAI has called for the US to work with countries around the world on international technical standards for frontier AI, drawing on the expertise of AI safety institutes and standards bodies. Common approaches to evaluating capabilities, assessing risks, testing safeguards and reporting incidents can help countries compare evidence and respond to risks that cross borders. The collaboration with NASK reflects the value of bringing national expertise into this wider effort.

In NASK’s case, this expertise rests on extensive research in AI safety, applied directly to protecting public services and Poland’s digital information ecosystem. Without national partners like NASK, global AI safety standards may remain detached from the realities in which AI is actually used.

Industry observers note that the agreement also builds on OpenAI’s existing work with cyber defenders in Poland. In July, CERT Polska, which operates within NASK, gained access⁠(opens in a fresh window) to OpenAI’s cyber capable models through Daybreak. The team used OpenAI models to help discover six vulnerabilities in MikroTik RouterOS, including flaws that could be combined to take control of affected devices without authentication. The vendor released fixes, which CERT Polska confirmed prevented the attacks it observed.

arXiv:2611.26809v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Modern language models (LMs) are increasingly deployed with access to search tools at inference. Yet pretraining remains predominantly focused on predicting static text, with search capabilities typically introduced during post-training. We propose Search-Native Pretraining as a practical route to teach search capability during pretraining from ordinary text corpora. Specifically, we augment pretraining corpus at scale with web-search queries and retrieve web response using a local index. Training on this augmented corpus teaches models to generate search calls and incorporate retrieved evidence during language modeling. Across Wikipedia and DCLM-Edu corpora and 360M to 3.3B parameter scales, search-pretrained models ("QueryLM") show improved performance on knowledge-intensive tasks and higher steerability toward the retrieved evidence. Crucially, their advantage persists after supervised fine-tuning of both search-pretrained and conventionally pretrained models, indicating that the tested post-training procedures do not fully recover the capabilities developed during pretraining. Throughout our experiments, we find that a 1.4B QueryLM consistently beats or matches the performance of a FLOP-matched 3.3B baseline model across all knowledge intensive tasks. These results establish search-pretraining as a practical way to develop foundational search capabilities during pretraining. We release the training artifacts, including model checkpoints and data.

AltRA-Test: An Alternative Annotator Test for LLM Judges Without Shared Annotators

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (280 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Industry observers note that arXiv:2611.26073v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as judges and graders to replace human annotators, raising the question of when such replacement is statistically justified. To support such decisions, the Alternative Annotator Test (Alt-Test) was introduced for dense settings where all items are annotated by the same annotators. However, in many large-scale annotation settings, items are annotated by different subsets of annotators. We therefore propose the Alternative Annotator Test with Resampled Annotations (AltRA-Test), a statistical test that does not require that all items are annotated by the same annotators. AltRA-Test uses a bootstrap that resamples items, draws k human annotations for each item, and substitutes one of them with an LLM annotation. This produces paired all-human and mixed human-LLM panels. A replacement is supported when the inter-annotator agreement (IAA) of the mixed panel is statistically non-inferior to the IAA of the all-human panel, i.e., when the LLM preserves the signal that the human annotators share. We establish that AltRA-Test is a consistent test of asymptotic level alpha. We then evaluate it through simulations and real-world experiments in which we test 18 LLMs and 5 prompting techniques on 20 datasets across text, image, audio, and video. Across these evaluations, about 100 items often suffice for the test. In simulations, where we know whether the LLM is a better or a worse annotator than the humans, AltRA-Test makes more correct replacement decisions than existing baselines. In real-world data experiments, LLMs pass the test in about half of the setups, depending mainly on the task. Since replacement is not always justified, we encourage researchers to test it for their task.

Replay, Don't Resample: Off-Policy Consolidation of Long-Horizon RL Experts

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (285 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Sources indicate that arXiv:2611.24059v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Frontier post-training follows a common recipe: train one expert per domain with reinforcement learning (RL), then consolidate the experts into one model via multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD). Such consolidation is expensive: the student samples in every environment again, an expert scores every sampled token, and the student inherits the drift of the final experts. Yet we argue that the experts' RL runs have already produced what consolidation needs: rollouts with their sampling probabilities and rewards, in the order the experts learned from them. We propose multi-expert replay policy distillation (MRPD), which replays these training logs through the student in the experts' order. At each step, the policy gradient is recomputed on these scored trajectories, and the final experts' distributions are distilled at the logged prefixes. Following the experts' own trajectory reduces the training-inference mismatch and keeps the student within the clip range, so the replay is off-policy in origin but quasi-on-policy throughout consolidation. MRPD samples nothing and calls no environment or reward model: the trainer is the sole process, and consolidating the experts costs only about a seventh of the compute used to train them. On three long-horizon agentic domains (reasoning, search and SQL), MRPD yields the best student model, substantially outperforming online RL baselines, and surpassing MOPD from the same experts at a fraction of MOPD's cost. Our analysis on the same logs demonstrates that the replayed trajectories carry most of the gain, and that both the policy gradient and the distillation term add to it. Most interestingly, the order of the logs matters more than their amount or rewards, suggesting that expert training logs are a curriculum, not a data mixture.

According to recent reports, arXiv:2611.22138v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Multimodal agents can now control robot arms by calling tools and writing code. Existing benchmarks fall short in three ways: most test one or two arms on short tasks, many pause the world while the agent thinks, and many give it ground-truth object positions. We present RoboTeam, a simulated benchmark where agents control 4 to 16 robot arms in real time from camera images alone. Its 36 tasks are long jobs that the arms must do together, such as passing timbers or building a picture from hundreds of cubes. We start from the most flexible agent system, the adaptive system, where one agent decides when to fork delegates. With it, gpt-6.1-sol and opus-5.5 complete 28 and 27 tasks, and four other models at most 3. But at a high price: a typical task takes gpt-6.1-sol 3.5 hours and 218 million input tokens, and a third of its steps fail at least once and must be retried. We then compare it with three fixed systems: single-agent, hierarchical, and decentralized. All four complete a similar number of tasks but differ in time and tokens. The hierarchical and decentralized systems are faster but use up to 1.9 times the tokens, and the single agent uses fewer tokens but takes 1.6 times as long, so the adaptive system lies between them. Even so, no model or system is yet fast, cheap, and reliable at once. RoboTeam measures these limits where earlier benchmarks cannot: long multi-arm jobs, camera images only, and a world that never pauses.

Sources indicate that patient requests, clinical letters, and consultation notes all create work that care teams must review and act on. When that work builds up, patients can wait longer for a response, and important information can sit in queues.

Recent findings suggest that anima⁠(opens in a latest window) brings these workflows into one platform, with specialized AI teammates that gather patient histories, process documents, and draft clinical notes for care teams. Its vision is personalized healthcare for everyone, guided by the conviction that care should follow need.

Anima began in the UK, where it now serves over 14 million patients across more than 1,000 clinics and processes more than 800,000 cases a month. It’s expanding into the US, Australia, and beyond. The firm uses GPT‑6 models in its document workflows and GPT‑Live for calls, selecting OpenAI after benchmarking all closed-source and open-source models, according to Shun Pang, Anima’s CEO and co-founder.

“We chose OpenAI for Anima’s mission-critical workloads because of superior intelligence, intelligence per dollar, and steerability with in-context learning.”.

Before he started Anima, Shun had gone through clinical training, where he saw a patient miss potentially life-saving care because abnormal test results sat in a queue for six months. He came to believe that the problem with healthcare wasn’t about medicine, but about how information moved through the system. He built Anima to give care teams more capacity to respond to patients’ needs. The platform brings patient requests, clinical documents, and follow-up work into one place.

Anima’s AI receptionist, Andi, is built on GPT‑Live. Patients can describe their symptoms over the phone to Andi, while Anima’s proprietary policy engine guides the conversation through deterministic, clinically approved intake workflows. GPT‑5.4 mini then selects the appropriate questionnaire, and the completed medical history appears as a structured case in the clinic dashboard. Doctors and clinic staff can review the case and take action from there.

According to recent reports, anima reports that clinics using Andi have reduced phone waits from 40 to 50 minutes to 10 minutes, a reduction of at least 75%. In Anima’s patient surveys, 86% said they would use Andi again. Anima found that people in their 80s and 90s were among its happiest customers. “They’re very happy to talk to a voice agent,” says Shun. “It’s infinitely patient and very polite.”.

Anima’s Documents product uses GPT‑6 models to extract information from incoming clinical documents such as the sender, recipient, document type, and event dates. A multi-stage pipeline then matches each document to the correct patient, identifies the appropriate clinical codes, and suggests the next action for clinic staff to review.

Clinical coding proved to be one of the hardest technical problems to solve. “There are around 800,000 possible SNOMED codes,” says Michael Skupien, Engineering Lead at Anima. “Only a fraction are used regularly, but different practices still make different decisions about which codes to use.”.

Rather than ask clinics to configure the system or fine-tune separate models for each customer, Anima uses in-context learning to adapt model decisions to each practice. This approach requires models that can follow instructions consistently.

According to Anima, practices that used to process about 15 documents per hour typically process 30 to 45. Top-performing clinics process 45 to 60. “We’ve seen clinics clear document backlogs of more than 100,000 documents within days of adopting Anima,” notes Shun. “That means important updates and medication changes reach clinicians promptly instead of sitting in a queue for months.”.

It has been revealed that as patients share critical information, doctors need to split their attention between listening and taking notes for the medical record. Anima built its Scribe product with GPT 5.6 Luna to turn consultation transcripts into structured clinical notes, and then reuse that same clinical context to draft referral letters and patient follow-up messages.

According to recent reports, instead of typing throughout the appointment, a doctor can give more of their attention to the patient. Anima reports that consultation notes that once took several minutes to write are drafted in seconds for the clinician’s review. Referral letters that often required 5 to 15 minutes to produce can also be drafted within seconds from the consultation and patient record, ready for the clinician to review.

“Patients receive clear follow-up messages shortly after the consultation, reducing anxiety and improving recall,” indicates Shun. “We often hear that doctors now finish their day on time instead of working until 8 or 9 p.m.”.

Anima’s vision is personalized healthcare for everyone. That requires care teams to have the information, time, and capacity to understand each person’s needs and act on them across the whole patient journey.

Its work with OpenAI models supports practical steps towards that vision. Andi gathers information over the phone and turns it into structured requests for staff to act on. Documents helps teams process incoming clinical information. Scribe drafts notes and follow-up communications for clinicians to review.

Anima reports that most cases across its platform are resolved within 24 hours, with a median resolution time of approximately 3.5 hours. “We’re having a huge impact on 14 million patients in the UK supported by OpenAI’s models,” Shun indicates. “It’s really mission-critical for the patients and the clinics.”.

Anima gives teams more room to care today, and helps them build pathways and services for the future.

The Silent Cost of Conversation History in LLM Reasoning

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (210 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.20071v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) in multi-turn information systems accumulate their own earlier replies and a growing task state. We asked whether this conversation history lowers accuracy, and whether process-level quality metrics warn before it does. Each analysis was fixed before its outcomes were computed. In Study 1, on 48 sharded math tasks, retaining its replies lowered final success by 0.21 for GPT-4o-mini and 0.29 for Mistral-7B (Holm-adjusted p = 0.026 and 0.004); Llama-4 Scout showed the same direction, not significant. Study 2 introduces CDR-Stream, 100-turn state-tracking dialogues with an exact answer per turn and per-model difficulty calibration. With the full history, accuracy fell from about 0.6 to 0.1 within twenty turns at matched difficulty, whereas a solver-verified state summary kept it 0.52-0.59 higher (Holm-adjusted p less than 0.001). Consistency and logical coherence fell far less than accuracy, and stability rose. None of these metrics, a paired readiness measure or calibrated single-stream drift detectors gave robust, model-general early warning, although in Study 2 the repeat-based metrics were complete only for GPT-4o-mini. In the monitors we tested, a single 100-turn stream had power only for very large drops. Systems built on LLMs should keep task state outside the transcript and monitor across sessions.
